===== FILE: ARCHITECTURE.md =====
# ARCHITECTURE: iTaK Torch Rebuild

Written 2026-10-29, on David's order of the same day: fix everything the
audits found, rebuild with Rust where the hot path needs it, take whatever
is needed from the old project, and get Glimmer working 100 percent on our
own stack. This file is the blueprint the build follows. PLAN.md says why
and in what order at the product level; TODO.md carries the work items;
this file fixes the module grid, the seam between the two processes, and
the design rules that close every audited gap by construction rather than
by patch.

## 1. Fixed decisions (settled, not reopened here)

- The split (David, 2026-10-27, DECISIONS.md): Rust owns the hot token
  loop. Go owns platform, API, scheduling, caches, cluster, and training
  orchestration. Two processes, one seam: a Unix domain socket carrying
  NDJSON frames for everything, control, tensors, and token streams
  alike; there is no shared-memory data plane (Section 4).
- Mojo stays the lab. Flutter is the console. Neither is on the serving
  path.
- First-class architecture target number one is muse-glimmer (Glimmer).
  The other families follow through the same arch seam, in the order the
  stages below set. (PLAN S13, TODO Phase 9; this settles the open
  question parked in PLAN S12.)
- David's build law applies to every module from birth: modular grid,
  debugging and linting built in (diagnostics, structured logs, a way to
  pull the bug information out, lint gates green), limits as config with
  defaults and never compiled constants, version fields in every data
  format, interface seams at every change-prone boundary.

## 2. The shape

Two processes on one host (the seam also works across hosts later; the
transport does not care):

| Process | Language | Owns | Never does |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| torchd (platform) | Go | HTTP API, auth, scheduling, batching policy, caches, model operations, cluster, training orchestration, observability | Token math, weight math, anything inside the per-token loop |
| itak-engine | Rust | Model loading, tokenization, the forward pass, sampling, KV state, speculative execution, GPU backends | HTTP, tenancy decisions, anything that requires knowing who asked |

The engine is replaceable without touching the platform and the platform
is replaceable without touching the engine. That is the point of the
seam, and it is also the fix for the old tree's core defect: in the old
tree the platform and a demo engine were fused, so the demo's limits
became the product's limits.

## 3. Module grid

### 3.1 Rust engine crates (the hot path)

| Module | Owns (its grid slot) | Interface | Depends on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| itak-types | The shared contracts of the Section 4 protocol: requests, responses, sampling params, errors, every struct carrying a version field; the Go side mirrors them in platform/internal/engine | Pure data; both sides compile against the same shapes | Nothing |
| itak-diag | Structured logging and the diagnostic channel: every refusal, fallback, and verdict in the engine emits here with a stable code | `diag!(code, fields)` macros; a diagnostics dump endpoint on the control socket | itak-types |
| itak-gguf | GGUF parsing and mmap weight access. The full mainline ggml type table (Section 5.2). Produces a load coverage report for every file | `load(path) -> ModelFile + CoverageReport`; any gap is an error value, never a silent default | itak-types, itak-diag |
| itak-loader | Turns a ModelFile into an in-memory model by asking the arch module for its tensor map and verifying every required tensor arrived, readable, right shape | `build(file, arch) -> Model` or a named load error listing exactly what is missing | itak-gguf, itak-arch |
| itak-arch | One submodule per architecture family, keyed on the file's own `general.architecture` string (Section 5.3). Each declares its tensor map, metadata keys, norm layout, activation, RoPE parameters, and KV shape | `ArchModule` trait: `tensor_map()`, `config(file)`, `forward hooks` | itak-types, itak-gguf |
| itak-arch::muse_glimmer | The Glimmer module (Section 6): 52-layer hybrid schedule, SWA rings, softcap, DFlash companion | Same ArchModule trait, no special cases outside it | itak-arch, itak-kv, itak-kernels |
| itak-tokenizer | Real tokenizers: byte-level BPE (GPT-2 style) and SentencePiece, pretokenizers including the llama4 pre-tokenizer, byte-level detokenization | `encode(text) -> ids`, `decode(ids) -> text`, both round-trip tested | itak-types |
| itak-kv | KV state: paged cache for global layers, fixed ring buffers for sliding-window layers, prefix-cache snapshots, versioned save and load that either works or errors | `KvStore` trait per layer kind; snapshot format carries a version field | itak-types, itak-diag |
| itak-kernels | The math: dequant for every type in the table, GEMV and GEMM, RMSNorm, RoPE, softmax, attention (paged and ring). CPU SIMD first; shape-specialized fused kernels for Glimmer land in Stage 4 | Pure functions over tensor views; allocation-free inside the token loop | itak-types |
| itak-backend | Hardware backends behind one trait: CPU SIMD (always available), wgpu on Vulkan (the 7900 XTX path). Hardware detection reads AMD VRAM from sysfs | `Backend` trait; `detect() -> HardwareReport` | itak-kernels, itak-diag |
| itak-forward | The incremental transformer step: one token in, logits out, KV updated in place. RoPE, final norm, per-family epsilon and activation all come from the arch module | `step(session, token) -> logits` | itak-arch, itak-kv, itak-kernels, itak-backend |
| itak-spec | Speculative execution: DFlash block drafting for Glimmer, n-gram prompt lookup, Medusa heads loaded from versioned artifact files | `draft(session) -> candidates`, `verify(...)`; every mode is config-gated and every gate has a behavior test | itak-forward, itak-arch |
| itak-engine (binary) | Session and slot management inside the engine, the IPC server side of the seam, sampling execution, EOS and stop handling | The IPC contract (Section 4) | All of the above |

### 3.2 Go platform packages

| Module | Owns (its grid slot) | Interface | Depends on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| platform (the Go module) | The platform half of the repo as one module, `github.com/David2024patton/itak-torch-rebuild/platform`. The Section 4 contracts are mirrored in internal/engine's client types; structured logging is slog throughout; diagnostics live in internal/diag | Builds platform/cmd/torchd | Nothing |
| platform/internal/engine | The Go side of the seam: the Client interface and the Unix-socket client for the protocol of Section 4 (hello, ping, debug, generate, embed, chat_template), handshake and protocol version check, named errors, bounded frame reads. Builds the sampling block of the Generate message from the request parameters | `Client.Generate(ctx, req) -> stream of token events` | Nothing (the seam itself) |
| platform/internal/server | HTTP surface: OpenAI-compatible chat, completions, embeddings, models; SSE streaming, validation, error mapping, generation caps. Auth middleware in front of every route group; startup diagnostics list every registered route | HTTP; binds 127.0.0.1 by default, LAN exposure only by explicit flag | platform/internal/engine, platform/internal/auth, platform/internal/scheduler, platform/internal/cache |
| platform/internal/auth | The one API-key middleware: constant-time comparison, fails closed, repeated failures throttled per source. The key is configuration (TORCH_API_KEY), never a file or a chat message | Middleware + identity context | Nothing |
| platform/internal/scheduler | The request scheduling gate: bounds how many engine jobs run at once and queues the rest in priority lanes, each lane capped at a configured number of waiters, every lane provably drained in every mode | Gate in the request path | platform/internal/engine |
| platform/internal/cache | Exact-match response cache: a TTL on every entry, an entry cap with expiry-first eviction, a purge janitor, an injectable clock. Cache keys are caller-built and carry the tenant dimension | Lookup and store hooks in the request path | Nothing |
| platform/internal/chattemplate | Renderer for the model's own GGUF chat template: a bounded Jinja subset with render budgets, so a hostile template refuses by name instead of hanging or blowing the stack | `Render(template, messages) -> prompt text` | Nothing |
| platform/internal/supervisor | Engine process lifecycle: start, health wait, restart within a budget, an allowlisted child environment (PATH plus ITAK_ENGINE_* only) | Process management used by platform/cmd/torchd | platform/internal/engine |
| platform/internal/diag | The diagnostics registry behind /debug: request counts per route, error counts, and engine call outcomes reported by every module | Snapshot served at /debug | Nothing |
| platform/cmd/torchd | The platform daemon binary: flags, env, signals, wiring. Every serving limit is a flag with its default recorded | CLI flags | All of the above |

Not yet built, and nothing in the tree answers for them yet: the
feature tier (guardrails, A/B and payload routing, versioning,
tracing), model operations (HF and OCI pulls, SHA-256 integrity,
versioning, warmup, prefault, GGUF export; quantize tools either
produce the file or exit non-zero), cluster coordination (join
requires the shared secret and an allowlisted address; no automatic
LAN discovery by default), and the training stack (an HTTP training
API over a real orchestration handle, and the orchestration itself:
autograd, optimizers, SFT, LoRA, DPO, GRPO, ORPO, QAT,
checkpointing). They keep their stages in Section 7; a route or verb
that cannot work is not registered.

### 3.3 Off the serving path

| Module | Owner | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mojo lab engines | Mojo | Research: SSM variants, the Latent Engine experiments. Results file into REFERENCES and PLAN; nothing ships from the lab without a plan change |
| Flutter console | Flutter | Operator UI over the platform API |
| itak-dissect (tool) | Rust | Per-layer weight statistics and heat maps, the GGUF to .itf converter (Phase 8) |

## 4. The seam: Go and Rust IPC contract

As built (this section describes the shipped seam; the definition of
record is `crates/itak-engine/src/protocol.rs` on the Rust side and
`platform/internal/engine/unix.go` on the Go side, and SERVING.md
carries the same definition in prose):

Transport: a Unix domain socket. The engine binds the path given by
`--socket` / `ITAK_ENGINE_SOCKET` (default `/tmp/itak-engine.sock`)
and loads its one model at startup from `--model`; there is no
load-model message, and a model that fails to load, including at the
tensor coverage gate, exits the process non-zero, so a partial model
never serves. Everything crosses the socket: there is no
shared-memory data plane, and no tensor or token stream travels
anywhere else.

Framing and versioning:

- One JSON object per line (NDJSON). A frame is a single line. The
  engine's reader caps a line at the configured maximum frame size
  (`--max-frame-bytes` / `ITAK_ENGINE_MAX_FRAME_BYTES`, default
  4,194,304 bytes) and refuses an over-long line as a named
  `bad_frame` error and closes, instead of growing a buffer without
  bound; the Go client caps a frame at the same 4 MiB.
- The first frame on every connection is Hello:
  `{"op":"hello","proto":1,"client":"torch-platform"}`. The engine
  answers with a `hello_ack` frame carrying its protocol version
  (1) and a detail string. A peer speaking another version gets an
  `error` frame with code `protocol_mismatch`, and the Go client
  likewise refuses a hello_ack carrying any other version, so a
  mismatch fails by name, never by hang and never by silent
  downgrade. Any frame arriving before Hello is refused.
- Before the handshake, the engine checks the connecting process's
  uid from the kernel peer credentials (SO_PEERCRED): a different
  uid gets one `peer_refused` error frame and the connection closes
  at once.
- Every operational limit on the seam is config with a default,
  never a compiled constant: frame size (above), the engine's slot
  count (`--slots`, default 1) and bounded job queue (`--max-queued`,
  default 8), the default generation cap (`--default-max-tokens`,
  default 128), the embed batch limits (`--max-embed-inputs`,
  `--max-embed-tokens`), and the platform supervisor's restart
  budget for the engine process (TODO T-9.11).

Message set (one `op` per frame):

| Message | Direction | Carries |
| --- | --- | --- |
| hello / hello_ack | both | Protocol version (1) and the client name; the ack carries the engine's detail string. A version mismatch is the named `protocol_mismatch` error instead |
| ping / pong | Go to Rust, reply | Health probe and its reply |
| debug / debug_info | Go to Rust, reply | The engine's self-report: model identity, tensor coverage, and slot and job counters |
| generate | Go to Rust | Prompt text (the engine owns the tokenizer; the platform sends text, never token ids), model name, max_tokens, stop strings, and the sampling block: temperature, top_p, top_k, seed, presence and frequency penalties |
| token | Rust to Go | One streamed piece of the completion, on the same socket: text and token_id per frame. The final frame carries `done` true and `finish_reason` set to `stop` or `length`, with empty text |
| embed / embeddings | Go to Rust, reply | Input texts; the reply frame itself carries one vector per input, in input order: mean-pooled token embeddings from the model's own embedding table, L2-normalized, as JSON arrays |
| chat_template / chat_template | Go to Rust, reply | The request asks for the model's own chat template; the reply carries the template text from the GGUF metadata plus the bos and eos token texts. A model whose file carries no template gets the named `no_chat_template` error. The platform renders the template; the engine only serves it |
| error | Rust to Go | A named refusal: `code` and `message`. The platform maps bad_request, context_overflow, model_not_found, and protocol_mismatch to a client error; forward_failed, detokenize_failed, engine_died, unknown_op, bad_frame, and internal to a gateway error; and engine_busy (every slot running and the bounded queue full) to 503 |

There is no abort message and no session or state message: the
engine's slots and job queue are internal, and the platform cancels
a generation by closing its connection, which its client does when
the request context ends; the exchange on that connection ends with
it.

Failure semantics:

- Engine crash: the platform marks the engine unhealthy, restarts it
  within the configured budget, and fails in-flight requests with a
  named error. Nothing hangs waiting on a dead process.
- Load failure: the model does not serve. There is no partial model
  state anywhere in the design.
- Any fallback (CPU backend instead of GPU, speculation off) is an
  explicit, logged, queryable state, never a silent one.

## 5. Design rules that close the audited gaps

Each rule names the audit finding it closes (native audit C and M
numbers, platform audit, gates audit, live test F numbers) and the
module that owns the rule. The full evidence lives in the four reports
in ~/workspace/model-teardown/.

### 5.1 Correctness of generation

| Rule | Closes | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The tokenizer is a real BPE or SentencePiece implementation, loaded from the model's own files, with token-for-token conformance tests against reference outputs and lossless round-trip tests | Native C1, live test F2, the platform tokenizer finding (the Ġ defect: detokenization reverses byte-level encoding, Ġ back to space, byte tokens reassembled) | itak-tokenizer |
| RoPE is applied in the forward step with the arch module's base and scaling; the final norm runs before the LM head; RMSNorm epsilon, activation (SwiGLU, GEGLU, and family variants), norm positions (pre, post, QK-norm), and logit transforms (softcap, scale) all come from the arch module, never from hardcoded defaults | Native C4 | itak-forward, itak-arch |
| Decode is incremental: one token per step against a real KV cache. Full re-forward per token does not exist anywhere in the design | Native M2, live test F1 | itak-forward, itak-kv |
| Sampling parameters, grammar, JSON mode, and stop rules in a request reach the sampler that runs. A parameter the engine cannot honor is refused in the response, never silently ignored | Platform constrained-decoding finding | platform/internal/engine, itak-engine |
| Every config flag has a behavior test proving the flag changes behavior. A flag read only by a log line is a build failure | Native M6 (the UseSpeculative printf), platform dead-feature pattern | All modules; enforced by the gates (5.6) |

### 5.2 The loader tells the truth

| Rule | Closes | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The ggml type table uses mainline numbering, full stop: BF16 is 30. Fork-only types (the BitNet I2_S family) live in a namespaced extension table keyed by source, never by renumbering mainline IDs | Native M3, live test notes | itak-gguf |
| Readers exist for every type the dissected corpus contains: F32, F16, BF16, Q4_0, Q4_1, Q5_0, Q5_1, Q8_0, Q8_1, Q2_K, Q3_K, Q4_K, Q5_K, Q6_K, and the K-quant mixes as shipped | Native C3a, live test F5 | itak-gguf, itak-kernels |
| Load produces a coverage report: required tensors per the arch map, found, readable, shape-checked. Any miss fails the load with a named error listing the tensor. Random or placeholder weights do not exist in this codebase; there is no code path that invents a weight | Native C3, live test F3 and F4 | itak-loader |
| Missing or unrecognized metadata fails the load with the key named. Defaults that fabricate a model (the old vocab 32000, hidden 768 fallback) are forbidden; vocab resolves from the arch metadata or the tokenizer's token count, and the source is in the coverage report | Native m4, live test F4 (five of eight test models ran with a fabricated vocab) | itak-loader, itak-arch |
| Shape mismatches in matmul are errors with shapes attached, and quantized payloads are first-class in every kernel path. A kernel never indexes a payload field it has not checked | Live test F3 (the safeMatMul panics) | itak-kernels |

### 5.3 Architecture dispatch is real

| Rule | Closes | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Routing is by the file's own `general.architecture` string through the arch registry, and the registry is the only way a model loads. An unrecognized string is a named refusal listing what is supported | Native C2, live test F4 | itak-arch |
| Each arch module's tensor map covers what the family's files actually contain: fused QKV (Phi-3), attention biases (Qwen2, StarCoder2), post-attention and post-FFN norms (Gemma 2, OLMo 2), QK-norms (OLMo 2), tied embeddings (Gemma, StarCoder2), up/down-only MLPs (StarCoder2), MLA tensors and expert tensors read under the file's own arch prefix (DeepSeek: expert counts come from `deepseek2.*` keys, never a hardcoded `llama.*` key) | Live test M1 to M4 and F4, native C3c | itak-arch family modules |
| Registry configuration numbers are verified against the published configs at build time by a conformance test (the audit's fetched corrections are the seed data: Mixtral RoPE base 1000000, Phi-3 mini context 4096 with window 2047, LLaMA-1 context 2048, Gemma vocab 256128, DeepSeek V3 MLA fields present and its memory estimate computed from per-layer expert math, not a dense shortcut) | Native M4, M5, m1 to m3, m6 | itak-arch, gates |
| The serve path never routes by file size. Engine selection is by capability: arch support and backend availability, stated in the load result | Native M1 | model operations (not yet built), itak-engine |
| State save and load either persist and restore, verified by a round-trip test, or the verb does not exist. Silent no-op success is forbidden in every module | Native m5 (SaveKVCache no-ops), platform state endpoint finding | itak-kv, platform/internal/server |

### 5.4 Speculation and subsystems are wired or absent

| Rule | Closes | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Speculative decoding exists in exactly the modes the engine executes: DFlash block drafting (Glimmer), n-gram lookup, Medusa from trained artifact files. The generation loop calls the decoder; a draft model configured but not called is impossible by construction | Native M6, platform spec finding (draft loaded, never run) | itak-spec |
| Sliding-window attention, paged KV, and ring caches are the KV implementation itself, called by the forward step, not library ornaments beside it | Native M7 | itak-kv |
| Medusa heads are files with version fields, produced by the training stack, loaded and verified at load time. Zero-initialized heads are a load state the engine reports, never a silent default | Native M6, PLAN S6 | itak-spec, training stack (not yet built) |
| A CLI or endpoint that cannot do its work exits non-zero or returns an error saying so. Printing success for simulated output is forbidden (the itak-quant lesson) | Platform itak-quant finding | model operations (not yet built), all CLIs |
| Header comments and docs are checked against behavior in review; a module whose docs claim what its code does not do fails the gate | Native M8 | Gates (5.6) |

### 5.5 Security from birth

| Rule | Closes | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Every route group sits behind auth middleware from the first server commit. API keys are per-user and hashed at rest; keys reach people through secure links, never files or chat | Platform C1 | platform/internal/auth, platform/internal/server |
| The server binds 127.0.0.1 by default. Binding wider requires an explicit flag, and startup diagnostics state the bind and the auth state in one line | Platform C1 (0.0.0.0 under a localhost comment) | platform/internal/server |
| Filesystem paths from requests are confined to configured directories and validated (the old validatePath discipline, applied everywhere, including state save and load) | Platform C2 (arbitrary path state endpoints) | platform/internal/server, itak-kv |
| Cluster join requires the shared secret and an allowlisted peer address; there is no automatic LAN discovery unless a flag turns it on | Platform swarm finding | cluster (not yet built) |
| Tenant identity from auth is part of scheduler decisions and cache keys from the first version, so isolation is a property of the data flow, not a later layer | Platform tenant finding | platform/internal/auth, platform/internal/scheduler, platform/internal/cache |

### 5.6 Gates from birth

The old tree's gates were red or absent (gates audit: test panic masking
about 120 tests, 165 of 167 FFI tests skipping, no lint config anywhere,
an assembly ABI mismatch in a hot kernel, a mandatory undocumented
sibling folder to build at all). The rebuild's rules:

- The repo carries .golangci.yml and clippy configuration from Stage 0,
  plus CI that runs build, vet, lint, and tests on every push. A red
  gate stops the line; nothing commits on red (commit-gates skill).
- Every package carries tests in proportion to its risk, and the
  training stack carries tests from its first commit.
- Tests that skip for a missing environment piece fail CI unless the
  skip is an explicit, listed exception. A suite that is green because
  it did not run is a red suite.
- Hand-written assembly and unsafe kernels carry ABI conformance tests
  (the dotQ4BlockAVX2 lesson: declaration and assembly must agree, and a
  test, not vet alone, proves it).
- Dependencies are published and versioned. The build never requires an
  undocumented sibling checkout (the ../Core lesson); itak-core is a
  versioned module from Stage 0.
- The conformance corpus is the teardown set: the thirteen dissected
  GGUF files from the 2026-10-29 model teardowns, with expected outcomes
  per file recorded in the test data. Loader, tokenizer, and arch tests
  run against real files, not fixtures invented to pass.

## 6. Glimmer as the first-class target (PLAN S13)

The muse_glimmer arch module is specified from the dissection
(~/workspace/glimmer-blueprint/GLIMMER-DISSECTION.md), not from
assumptions:

| Fact from the file | Design consequence |
| --- | --- |
| 52 layers: 39 sliding-window (window 2048), 13 global at indices 3, 7, 11, up to 51 | The KV store is hybrid by construction: 39 fixed rings of 2048 slots, 13 paged global caches. Whole-context KV stays near 1.7 GiB at 131K, so KV work is deliberately minimal; the effort goes to weight streaming |
| Hidden 6656, FFN 19968, FFN is 75 percent of all bytes | The specialized kernels target exactly two shapes first: the FFN GEMV at 6656 by 19968 and the attention projections. Sensitivity-ranked quant handling starts at the FFN |
| 32 Q heads, 2 KV heads, head dim 128 | GQA at 16 to 1 is a first-class kernel case, not a generic path |
| RoPE base 500000 | From the arch module's config, read from file metadata |
| Logit softcap 20.0, logit scale 0.1961, untied Q5_K output head | Logit transform lives in the arch module; the Q5_K reader is on the critical path for this model, which is why 5.2 lists it by name |
| Vocab 202048, GPT-2 BPE with the llama4 pre-tokenizer | The tokenizer conformance set is Glimmer's own prompts first |
| Quant mix: Q4_K 77.3 percent, Q6_K 17.1 (ffn_down and attn_v alternate by layer half), Q5_K 5.5, F32 norms | Dequant kernels are tuned for this mix; the alternating Q6_K pattern is data in the coverage report, not a surprise |
| DFlash draft: own arch (dflash), 5 layers, block size 16, 1.51 GiB | itak-spec loads it as a companion through the same loader and arch seam; the draft depth sweep (parked T-P.1) runs against the new stack and its result is config, not code |
| mmproj vision tower, 1.30 GiB | Vision enters through the platform's modality routes after text is proven; the tower loads through the same loader rules |

The speed ladder, measured on the 7900 XTX against the recorded
baselines (llama.cpp Vulkan 44.31 tok/s plain, 88.6 effective with
DFlash, ceiling 60 plain at this quant):

1. Verified text on CPU (correctness before speed, always).
2. Verified text on the wgpu Vulkan backend.
3. Plain decode at or above 44.31 tok/s, then toward the specialized
   target near 51.
4. DFlash on the new stack at or above the 88.6 baseline, then the
   depth sweep.

A speed number without the verified-text proof at the same commit does
not count, in either direction.

## 8. Salvage manifest (what comes from the old project)

Taken, audited as it lands: the platform's working core concepts and
code (scheduler and slot batching, response and prefix caches, model
pulls and integrity checks, Ollama-compatible surface, GGUF converter),
the FFI speculative decoding logic as the reference for itak-spec
behavior, the trainer surface as the specification for the training
stack (not yet built), the
Mojo engines as lab artifacts, and the design record (the original PLAN,
DECISIONS, and research notes in this repo).

Rebuilt, not ported: the loader, the tokenizer, the forward pass, the
arch registry, and the KV subsystem. The audits showed these are the
parts whose old implementations cannot be repaired into correctness.

Dropped: the file-size routing rule, the placeholder quant CLI's
behavior (rebuilt to produce files or fail), every silent fallback, and
every feature claim with no wired code behind it. A feature enters the
README when its proof exists, not before.

## 9. Non-goals for this blueprint

- No llama.cpp FFI in the new engine. The FFI path stays available in
  the old tree as the reference implementation and the fallback serving
  path until Stage 4 proves the new stack; the version-lock fix for it
  (making the llama_params_fit prep optional) is old-tree maintenance,
  tracked outside this blueprint.
- ROCm and HIP stay parked per DECISIONS (2026-10-26); Vulkan via wgpu
  is the GPU path.
- Multi-GPU, tensor parallelism, and disaggregated serving are designed
  at the seam (the IPC contract does not forbid them) and built only if
  the single-card path proves out (PLAN S7).

===== FILE: BACKEND.md =====
# BACKEND: itak-backend scoping (wgpu on Vulkan, RX 7900 XTX)

Status: scoping document for TODO T-4.1 (Backend trait plus CPU SIMD
backend), T-4.2 (wgpu backend on Vulkan), and the hardware detection
proof inside T-9.5. ARCHITECTURE.md Section 3.1 owns the module
contract (`Backend` trait; `detect() -> HardwareReport`; depends on
itak-kernels and itak-diag). This document owns the internals: which
kernels, in which order, with what memory strategy, what happens when
the GPU path is not available, and the rule that would move us from
wgpu to raw Vulkan (ash). DECISIONS 2026-10-26 stands: ROCm and HIP
are parked; Vulkan is the GPU path.

## 1. Ground truth (measured 2026-10-28, bench/ and TODO T-0.2, T-P.2)

Speed anchors are harness-relative (DECISIONS.md, 2026-10-30); the
harness is named per number below, and the Section 9 sweep harness is
the designated comparison shape for operating-point claims.

| Fact | Value |
| :--- | :--- |
| Card | AMD Radeon RX 7900 XTX (Navi 31, RDNA3), 24 GiB |
| Memory bandwidth, hardware | 960 GB/s |
| llama.cpp Vulkan decode, Glimmer Q4_K_M (llama-bench, tg128 after pp512) | 44.31 tok/s = 708 GB/s achieved (73.8 percent of peak) |
| llama.cpp Vulkan decode with DFlash (2026-10-28 model-suite run, depth 4) | 88.6 effective tok/s |
| llama.cpp Vulkan decode, Glimmer Q4_K_M (Section 9 sweep harness: llama-server /completion, short raw prompts, fixed 256-token generations, temperature 0; measured 2026-10-30, bench/gpu-proof-2026-10-30.md) | 41.64 tok/s plain; DFlash depth 4 = 103.01, depth 6 = 107.39 effective tok/s (depth 6 is the operating point by the SPEC 9.4 rule) |
| HIP decode, same build | 41.13 tok/s (Vulkan keeps generation; HIP won prefill only) |
| Ceiling at this quant | 60.0 tok/s (14.89 GiB streamed per token) |
| Specialized target (ARCHITECTURE Section 6) | about 51 tok/s (85 percent of peak) |

Decode is a streaming problem: each token reads essentially every
weight byte once. Kernel work is therefore judged in GB/s first and
FLOPs never. 708 GB/s is the number to match; 960 GB/s is the
hardware wall nobody crosses.

## 2. Adapter probe (run 2026-10-29, on the server, wgpu 27.0.1)

A minimal wgpu probe (source in the Appendix) was built on this
workstation, copied to the server, and run there. It enumerates
adapters and prints the selected adapter's name, backend, and limits.
Enumeration only: it dispatched no work and touched no running
service. Full output condensed:

| # | Adapter | Backend | Type | Notes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 0 | AMD Radeon RX 7900 XTX (RADV NAVI31) | Vulkan | DiscreteGpu | vendor 0x1002, device 0x744c, RADV Mesa 26.0.8, Vulkan API 1.4.335 |
| 1 | Intel(R) UHD Graphics 770 (ADL-S GT1) | Vulkan | IntegratedGpu | the host iGPU |
| 2 | llvmpipe (LLVM 21.1.8, 256 bits) | Vulkan | Cpu | software rasterizer, always present with Mesa |

Selected under `PowerPreference::HighPerformance`: adapter 0, the
7900 XTX. Limits that shape the design, as granted by that adapter:

| Limit | 7900 XTX via wgpu | Design consequence |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| max_buffer_size | 2,147,483,647 (2 GiB minus 1) | No single weight buffer: Glimmer is 15.59 GiB. One storage buffer per tensor (largest single tensor, the Q5_K output head, is about 0.86 GiB and fits) |
| max_storage_buffer_binding_size | 2,147,483,647 | Binding slices are not a constraint on this stack; any tensor binds whole |
| max_compute_workgroup_storage_size | 65,536 (64 KiB LDS) | The 6656-wide hidden vector stages in LDS as f32 (26,624 B). The 19968-wide FFN intermediate does not (79,872 B f32); it fits as f16 (39,936 B) or the down projection reads it from L2 instead (Section 4) |
| max_compute_workgroups_per_dimension | 65,535 | One workgroup per output row cannot cover the 202,048-row output head in one dispatch dimension; kernels use two-dimensional dispatch or grid-stride loops |
| min/max subgroup size | 32 / 64 | RDNA wave32 is the native reduction unit; subgroup operations are available (Features::SUBGROUP present) |
| Features present | SUBGROUP, TIMESTAMP_QUERY, SHADER_F16 | Subgroup reductions, in-engine timestamp timing for the bench plan, and optional f16 staging all exist on this stack |
| max_bind_groups / dynamic storage buffers per layout | 8 / 8 | Ample for a matvec pipeline (weights, input, output, parameters) |

Two warnings the probe makes concrete:

1. **Selection is a policy, not a default.** This host exposes three
   Vulkan adapters. HighPerformance happened to pick the right one,
   but that is driver behavior, not a contract. `detect()` must rank
   DiscreteGpu on Vulkan first, reject `device_type: Cpu` outright
   (llvmpipe would report success while running slower than our own
   CPU backend, and its binding cap is the 128 MiB Vulkan floor), and
   record the chosen adapter in the HardwareReport and the diag
   channel.
2. **Request the adapter's limits, not wgpu's defaults.** A device
   created with wgpu's default limits caps buffers far below what
   RADV grants. `detect()` requests the adapter limits at device
   creation and verifies the granted limits against the kernel
   requirements; a shortfall is a fallback event (Section 6), never a
   surprise mid-load. Cross-check: sysfs
   `/sys/class/drm/card2/device/mem_info_vram_total` reads
   25,753,026,560 bytes (24,560 MiB) on this host, and the
   HardwareReport carries both the sysfs number (the fix for the old
   nvidia-smi-only detection bug) and the wgpu adapter identity; a
   disagreement between them is itself a diag event.

## 3. Kernel priority for decode

Order is by bytes streamed per token on Glimmer, then by position on
the critical path. All are fused dequantize-and-multiply GEMV kernels:
quantized blocks are expanded in registers and never materialized as
floating-point weights anywhere.

| Priority | Kernel | Glimmer shapes and share | Why this order |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| K1 | Q4_K dequant GEMV | FFN gate and up (6656 to 19968), attention Q and K projections, embedding; 77.3 percent of all bytes | The bulk of the stream. This kernel's GB/s is the backend's GB/s |
| K2 | Q6_K dequant GEMV | FFN down (19968 to 6656) and attn_v, alternating by layer half; 17.1 percent | Second-largest stream, and it consumes the FFN intermediate, so its input strategy (Section 4) is coupled to K1's epilogue |
| K3 | Q5_K dequant GEMV | The untied output head (6656 to 202,048); 5.5 percent of bytes | Small share but runs every token and produces the logits; the old loader could not even read this type. Includes the dispatch-dimension workaround (202,048 rows) |
| K4 | RMSNorm fused with residual add | 6656 wide, every layer, twice | Bytes are trivial; the point is fusion so the hidden vector is not re-read from VRAM between kernels |
| K5 | RoPE plus KV append | Q and K vectors, head dim 128 | Fused into the projection epilogue where the pipeline allows, else standalone; writes K and V into paged (global layers) or ring (sliding layers) slots in the same pass |
| K6 | GQA decode attention | 32 Q heads over 2 KV heads, head dim 128; ring variant (window 2048) and paged split-K variant for global layers | Attention reads about 78 MiB per token for the 39 sliding layers and up to 1.66 GiB per token for the 13 global layers at the full 131K context. Second-order at chat lengths, real at long context; split-K with online softmax and subgroup reductions |
| K7 | SwiGLU elementwise | 19968 wide | An epilogue of the up projection writing the activated intermediate, in f16 when the down projection will stage it in LDS |
| K8 | Embedding gather, logit softcap and scale | One row of 6656; 202,048 logits | Trivial kernels; the softcap (20.0) and scale (0.1961) come from the arch module and fuse into the K3 epilogue |

After decode: prefill GEMM variants of K1 to K3 (same block decoders,
M equal to the prefill chunk), and GPU kernels for the remaining
types in the ARCHITECTURE 5.2 table (Q8_0, Q5_0, Q8_1, Q4_0, Q4_1,
Q2_K, Q3_K, F16). Until a type has a GPU kernel it runs through the
per-op CPU fallback, disclosed at load time (Section 6). Sampling
stays on CPU at first: the logits vector is 0.8 MB, and moving it is
cheaper than a GPU top-k until batch sizes say otherwise.

Every kernel ships with its CPU SIMD reference beside it (T-4.1) and
a conformance test comparing GPU output against that reference on
real tensor data, per the repo rule that debugging and lint gates are
part of every module from birth.

## 4. Workgroup and memory strategy for a bandwidth-bound GEMV on RDNA3

- **Weights stream exactly once; activations are free by comparison.**
  A step's weight traffic is 14.89 GiB against kilobytes of
  activations. Every choice optimizes sequential read throughput:
  consecutive threads read consecutive packed words (vec4 loads of
  the block stream), and no kernel ever writes a dequantized weight.
- **Multiple output rows per workgroup.** A workgroup computes a
  small tile of output rows (4 to 8) for one projection. The
  activation vector is loaded into LDS once and reused across the
  tile, and one pass over the activation serves every row in the
  tile; weight bytes are untouched by this choice. Workgroup size 64
  or 128 (two to four wave32s); the exact tile is a tuning constant
  per kernel, recorded with its bench result, not a hidden default.
- **Dequantize along super-block boundaries.** Work is partitioned so
  a super-block's scale and min values are loaded once per workgroup
  tile and applied to every row's copy of that block in registers.
- **The down projection is the special case.** Its input is the
  19968-wide intermediate, which exceeds LDS in f32. Two candidate
  strategies, decided by the K2 bench: stage the intermediate in LDS
  as f16 (39,936 B, SHADER_F16 is present), or leave it in global
  memory where the 96 MiB Infinity Cache holds it trivially and skip
  staging. Split-K with a partials buffer is the third option if
  neither saturates; WGSL atomics are integer-only, so split-K
  reduction is a second small kernel, never an atomic shortcut.
- **Small-batch, not batch-1-only.** The engine serves multiple
  slots; kernels take M (tokens this step) as a parameter with the
  GEMV as M equals 1. Weights stream once per step regardless of M,
  so slot batching divides weight traffic per token. The CPU
  reference defines correctness for every M the GPU path accepts.
- **Per-tensor buffers, prebuilt bind groups.** Buffers are created
  once at load (Section 5). The per-token path records dispatches
  only: no allocations, no uploads except the step's token rows and
  KV appends, no pipeline creation (all pipelines compile at load,
  which also moves Naga translation cost out of the token loop).
- **Timestamps on.** TIMESTAMP_QUERY is present; kernels carry
  optional timestamp writes so the bench plan and later profiling
  read per-kernel time from inside the engine instead of guessing.

## 5. VRAM residency across the Go and Rust process split

- **The engine process owns the GPU, exclusively.** Only itak-engine
  creates a wgpu instance and device. The Go platform never links
  Vulkan, never opens the device, and never sees a tensor: the seam
  carries requests, token events, and health. A platform restart
  cannot disturb GPU state; an engine crash takes its device with it
  and the platform restarts the engine within its budget
  (ARCHITECTURE Section 4 failure semantics), after which weights
  re-upload from the mmap'd file. Cross-process device sharing and
  external-memory tricks are a non-goal.
- **Residency is all-or-nothing per model.** At load, the backend
  uploads every tensor of the model (plus companions: DFlash 1.51
  GiB, mmproj 1.30 GiB) into per-tensor storage buffers that live
  until unload. For Glimmer: 15.59 GiB of weights, 2.81 GiB of
  companions, about 1.7 GiB of KV at the full 131K context, plus
  workspace; roughly 20.5 GiB against the card's 24 GiB. If the
  budget does not fit (budget is sysfs VRAM total minus a configured
  reserve), the load refuses by name with the byte counts. There is
  no partial residency and no host-memory spill path: a weight that
  streams from system RAM mid-token silently destroys the bandwidth
  the design exists to protect.
- **Accounting is cross-checked.** The coverage report records
  per-tensor device bytes from the backend, and the load verifies
  the total against the sysfs VRAM-used delta. Weights are immutable
  after upload; LoRA adapters, when they arrive, are separate small
  buffers, never edits to resident tensors.
- **Coexistence is a rollout concern, not a backend feature.** The
  production llama-server holds VRAM on this host today. The backend
  reports free VRAM from sysfs before a load and refuses if the
  budget fails; pausing or restarting another process is the bench
  harness's etiquette under David's rules, never something the
  backend does on its own.

## 6. Fallback ladder

Per ARCHITECTURE Section 4: any fallback is an explicit, logged,
queryable state, never a silent one. Every transition below emits an
itak-diag event with the listed code (codes proposed here, to be
registered in itak-diag when the crate lands) and is visible in the
engine health the platform reads over the seam.

| Level | State | Trigger | Diag event |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| L0 | wgpu Vulkan on the discrete AMD adapter | Normal operation | `backend.selected` at startup (adapter name, backend, sysfs VRAM) |
| L1 | wgpu Vulkan on a non-discrete adapter | Only when configuration explicitly allows it | `backend.selected` with the adapter named; never entered by preference drift |
| L2 | Per-op CPU execution for a quant type with no GPU kernel yet | Decided at load from the coverage report, listed per (op, type) in the load result | `backend.op_fallback_cpu` per pair, at load |
| L3 | Device recreation, once | wgpu device-lost callback (driver reset, GPU hang) | `backend.device_lost`, then `backend.device_recreated` or escalation |
| L4 | CPU SIMD backend for everything | No suitable adapter, granted limits below kernel requirements, L3 recreation failed, or configuration disables the GPU | `backend.fallback_cpu` with a reason field |

A software adapter (llvmpipe) counts as no adapter: it lands on L4,
not on a pretend GPU level. The CPU SIMD backend is the correctness
reference for every kernel, is always compiled in, and is a
supported serving mode in its own right (T-4.1's proof: the engine
serves with the GPU backend disabled).

## 7. Measurement plan (against the 708 GB/s reference)

Correctness gates speed at every tier: a tier's numbers count only
with verified text (temperature 0 output matching the reference
engine on the bench prompt set) at the same commit, per ARCHITECTURE
Section 6. All results report effective bandwidth (tok/s multiplied
by 15.99 GB streamed per token at this quant) beside tok/s, at least
three runs, median reported, with card clocks, driver version, and
VRAM state recorded.

| Tier | What runs | Pass mark |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 0 | This adapter probe, rerun as a smoke check on driver or wgpu changes | The 7900 XTX is selected and granted limits match Section 2 |
| 1 | Stream micro-bench: a read-mostly kernel over Q4_K-shaped buffers totaling one model's stream (14.89 GiB across per-tensor buffers) | Establishes the wgpu stack's streaming ceiling. Below 637 GB/s (90 percent of llama.cpp's 708) after workgroup tuning triggers the ash evaluation in Section 8 |
| 2 | Per-kernel benches at exact Glimmer shapes (K1 gate and up, K2 down, K3 head), timestamps from inside the engine | Each kernel's GB/s recorded; the FFN pair and the head set the expectations for Tier 3 |
| 3 | Model level: T-4.2's bench table (CPU backend, wgpu backend, llama.cpp Vulkan from Phase 0), then T-9.5 with DFlash against the 88.6 baseline | Speed ladder steps in order: verified text on wgpu, then 44.31 tok/s parity, then toward 51 |

## 8. Risks, and the rule for switching to raw Vulkan (ash)

**wgpu's limits on this stack, as measured.** The probe retired the
scary version of this risk: buffer and binding caps (2 GiB) clear
our largest tensor, subgroups and f16 and timestamp queries are all
exposed on RADV, and LDS is a full 64 KiB. What remains is real but
narrower: the 65,535 workgroup dispatch cap forces grid discipline
in K3; wgpu caps are per-device defaults that must be raised
deliberately (Section 2); and wgpu adds a translation layer (WGSL
through Naga to SPIR-V, then RADV's compiler) whose codegen we do
not control instruction by instruction. A Naga or driver update can
move performance without any change in our code, which is why Tier 1
is the standing tripwire on dependency and driver bumps.

**Shader authoring cost per quant type.** Each K-quant layout is a
different block decoder: Q4_K packs eight sub-block scale and min
pairs into a 256-weight super-block, Q5_K adds a separate high-bits
plane, Q6_K carries sixteen int8 scales under one f16 super-scale.
The GEMV skeleton (tiling, LDS staging, reduction) is shared; the
decoder is not. Budget half a day to two days per type including
validation against the CPU reference. The decode-critical set is
three types (Q4_K, Q5_K, Q6_K cover Glimmer completely); the rest of
the 5.2 table can arrive one at a time behind the L2 fallback, each
announced at load. Shape specialization multiplies testing, not
shaders: tile sizes are tuning constants, and only the two FFN
shapes and the output head earn dedicated tuning.

**The decision rule for ash.** Evaluate a raw-Vulkan path behind the
same Backend trait if, and only if, at least one trigger fires:

1. Tier 1 lands below 637 GB/s after workgroup tuning (the wgpu
   abstraction is costing more than 10 percent of the bandwidth
   llama.cpp already achieves on this card), or
2. a capability gap blocks a required kernel on RADV through wgpu
   (a limit that cannot be raised to the adapter's real value, a
   missing feature the kernels genuinely need), or
3. a per-kernel gap above 5 percent against hand-tuned expectations
   is traced to Naga codegen and cannot be closed from WGSL.

If a trigger fires, the evaluation is one prototype: K1 in ash at
Glimmer shapes, adopted only if it beats the wgpu kernel by more
than 5 percent at Tier 2 or removes the blocking gap. Kernel callers
sit above the Backend trait either way, so the swap, if it ever
happens, is local to this crate. Until a trigger fires, wgpu stays:
it removes hand-rolled synchronization and descriptor management
from a one-card product, and the measured limits say it is not the
bottleneck standing between us and 708 GB/s.

## BACKEND-RESULTS: K1 first landing (2026-10-29, crate `wgpu-compute`)

The wgpu member of the itak-backend family landed as its own
crate beside `cpu-compute` (the way the CPU member landed for
T-4.1): `crates/wgpu-compute`, implementing `muse_glimmer::Compute`
with device selection per Section 2 and kernel K1 real. K2 to K8
sit in their own modules under the crate's `kernels` map, and
every step that needs one refuses through that module with a
named `StepFailed`; nothing falls back silently inside a step
(Section 6's L2 composition stays a caller decision).

**Correctness.** Synthetic full-row tests compare the GPU result
against the `gguf` crate's dequantizer plus `torch-math` within
reassociation noise, and the `k1_check` example ran the real
file's `blk.0.ffn_gate.weight` ([6656 x 19968], 74,760,192 bytes)
through `proj` on the server: max relative error 2.98e-7, cosine
1.000000000 against the CPU reference. The Q6_K refusal through
K2 and the cached-name geometry refusal are pinned by tests.

**Bench method.** Server, RX 7900 XTX via RADV Mesa 26.0.8, wgpu
27.0.1. The bench (`k1_bench` example) holds real Q4_K tensors
resident and dispatches the GEMV over all of them per iteration:
6 tensors, 167,731,200 bytes streamed per iteration, 2,000 timed
iterations after 50 warmup, median of 3 runs. Short windows
mislead on this card: an early 25-iteration run (a 68 ms window)
read 61.4 GB/s before clocks ramped, so no number below comes
from a short window; the single-tensor probe's timed window is
about 0.2 s at its speed, the resident-set runs about 1.5 to
2.3 s.

| Measurement | GB/s | Note |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Stream probe (this grid and access pattern, no dequant math; `stream_probe` example) | 746.9 | The wgpu stack's streaming level on this card |
| K1 v1: scalar byte loads, one row per workgroup | 148.6 | First version |
| K1 v2: vec4 traffic, one lane per super-block (SHIPPED) | 216.5 | The kernel in the crate |
| K1 v3: Section 4 tile (4 rows per workgroup, activations staged in workgroup memory) | 147.6 | Built, measured, rejected: staging cost more than shared activation loads saved at these shapes |

**Ash verdict (Section 8 rule, computed).** The shipped K1 lands
at 216.5 GB/s, which is 30.6 percent of llama.cpp's 708 GB/s and
below the 637 GB/s trigger: by the rule as written, the ash
evaluation trigger FIRES for K1 after tuning. The evidence
complicates the trigger's premise, and the complication is
recorded rather than smoothed over: the stream probe through
the same wgpu stack, same grid, reached 746.9 GB/s (105 percent
of llama.cpp's number), so the gap is not the abstraction's
streaming cost; it is the dequant instruction mix inside the
kernel (nibble extraction, per-element conversion, and the
factored scale/min sums). Section 8's prescribed prototype (K1
in ash at Glimmer shapes) remains one valid next experiment; a
llama.cpp-style kernel restructure in WGSL (shared-memory
dequant staging, per-thread K slices) is the other, and the
probe says the stack would not be its ceiling. No ash work was
started under this landing; the trigger state is the record.

**Residency notes.** Nothing hit the 2 GiB buffer cap: the
largest K1 tensor is 74.8 MB, and the cap first matters at K3's
0.86 GiB head, which fits. The bench window itself was
constrained: the production llama-server held 25.35 GB of the
card's 25.75 GB VRAM (about 384 MiB free), so the bench ran with
a 160 MiB resident subset (still roughly twice the 96 MiB
Infinity Cache, so the stream is VRAM traffic) instead of the
full 14.89 GiB model stream. A full-residency Tier 1 run needs
the card to itself and is a scheduled measurement, not a bench
beside production. Coexistence is a first-order effect on this
host: later the same evening, with a second llama-server and
engine processes from parallel work on the card, the identical
bench binary read about 17 GB/s. Bench reports on this host
must state their window, as this one does.

## BACKEND-RESULTS: the K1 tuning pass (2026-10-30)

The v2 kernel (one workgroup per row, one lane per super-block)
was restructured in llama.cpp's own direction. What was adopted
from the ggml-vulkan sources on the server
(`~/llama.cpp/ggml/src/ggml-vulkan/`, read before writing):

- `mul_mat_vec_q4_k.comp`: sixteen threads cooperate on one
  super-block, each owning sixteen elements (two `u32` qs
  words) unpacked by byte-unpack into vec4s, with the
  scale/min arithmetic factored against per-sub-block
  activation sums.
- `ggml-vulkan.cpp`: on RDNA3 the row split for K-quants is
  `rm_kq` 2 rows per workgroup (4 is GCN only); the large
  variant runs subgroup size times four threads (128 here)
  with a hybrid subgroup plus shared-memory reduction.
- The tuned kernel is therefore: two rows per workgroup of
  128, sixteen threads per super-block, packed extraction of
  the twelve scale bytes into per-sub-block scale/min in one
  unpack per half, activation quads loaded once per
  super-block and shared by both rows and all sixteen lanes,
  subgroup butterfly reduction with an LDS finish (a plain
  LDS tree variant remains as the no-subgroup fallback,
  selected at device setup from granted features).

One directed idea was evaluated and rejected on paper, with
the reasoning recorded so it is not retried blind: shared
memory DEQUANT STAGING. A GEMV consumes every dequantized
value exactly once, so staging dequantized tiles in workgroup
memory buys a barrier and a round trip for zero reuse; scale
staging loses the same way, because all sixteen lanes extract
their scales in parallel in the same instruction slots one
staging lane would spend serially. ggml's GEMV stages nothing
either; its shared memory carries reduction partials, as does
the tuned kernel's.

### Correctness first (real tensor, before any bench counted)

`k1_check` on the real `blk.0.ffn_gate.weight` [6656 x 19968]
Q4_K against the `gguf` crate's CPU dequant plus matvec
(pass bar: max rel err below 1e-4 and cosine above 0.999999;
f32 reassociation in a different order lands around 1e-6, so
the bar leaves two orders of headroom and still catches any
layout error, which is off by whole dequantized values):

| Shape | Max rel err | Cosine | Verdict |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | :--- |
| v2 (legacy) | 2.980e-7 | 1.000000000 | pass |
| r1, r2, r4 (LDS reduction) | 1.341e-7 | 1.000000000 | pass |
| r2sg, r4sg (subgroup) | 1.267e-7 | 1.000000000 | pass |
| r2f16 | 5.869e-4 | 0.999999621 | FAIL |
| r4sgf16 | 5.870e-4 | 0.999999621 | FAIL |

The first check round caught a real defect in the new shader:
every llama shape read the qs plane one word early (the plane
starts at word 4, after `d`, `dmin` and the twelve scale
bytes); v2 passing while all new shapes failed identically is
what isolated it to the port, not the design.

The f16 result is the tolerance call the pass owed: the f16
shapes hold per-sub-block dots in f16 and combine in f32
(strictly tighter than ggml's f16 pipeline, whose running
temp is f16), and they still land at rel 5.9e-4 on the real
tensor, outside the crate's 1e-4 bar. f16 activations are
therefore NOT taken: the variants remain benchable under
explicit names, they are never selected by `shipped_shape`,
and the bench below shows the rejection cost nothing, because
both f16 shapes also measured SLOWER than their f32 twins on
this card (activation traffic was never the bottleneck once
the dequant mix was fixed).

### The two windows (read this before the numbers)

This host produced two disjoint bench windows in one night,
and the difference is the window, proven three ways: the
first landing's own v2 binary re-read 24.4 GB/s in the bad
window against its 216.5 from the good one; the dequant-free
stream probe read 12.8 GB/s in the bad window against 746.9
in a good one; and per-process GPU engine counters showed no
tenant computing during the bad window's matrix (the same
effect the first landing's residency note recorded at about
17 GB/s under parallel tenants). In the bad window (around
04:29 UTC, VRAM free 98 MiB, two Qwen3-Embedding llama-servers
and production resident) every kernel compressed toward a
~140 GB/s ceiling: probe 12.8, v2 24.4, and the llama shapes
137.2 to 141.0, medians of three at 6,000 iterations on a
93,929,472-byte subset. That matrix is kept in the bench log
and carries exactly one usable signal: inside one window, the
restructure beat v2 by about 5.7 times. No absolute from that
window is used anywhere in the verdict.

The healthy window opened minutes later (around 04:44 UTC)
after the co-tenants released the card (VRAM free 2,824 MiB,
production resident and answering `/health` before and
after). One caution for future bench work on this host:
`pp_dpm_mclk` read 96 MHz in BOTH windows, including during
816 GB/s runs that are physically impossible at that memory
clock, so the sysfs clock readout is unreliable evidence
here; a same-window stream-probe canary is the test that
counts, and a canary under roughly 100 GB/s means the
window, not the kernel, is the story.

### Healthy-window matrix (the verdict numbers)

Established harness discipline: the six largest Q4_K tensors
as the resident set (160 MiB budget, 167,731,200 bytes
streamed per iteration, the same set as the first landing),
6,000 timed iterations plus 200 warmup (longer than the
first landing's 2,000 plus 50), median of three runs, every
run within 0.3 percent of its siblings:

| Shape | Median GB/s | Note |
| :--- | ---: | :--- |
| v2 (legacy) | 342.6 | same kernel as the 216.5 landing; windows differ |
| r1 (1 row, LDS) | 713.3 | the restructure alone already clears 708 |
| r2f16 | 737.6 | tolerance-failed AND slower than r2 |
| r4 (4 rows, LDS) | 770.7 | |
| r2 (2 rows, LDS) | 779.0 | |
| r4sgf16 | 780.1 | tolerance-failed |
| r4sg (4 rows, subgroup) | 794.3 | |
| r2sg, workgroup 64 | 802.9 | spot check |
| r2sg, workgroup 256 | 808.9 | spot check |
| **r2sg, workgroup 128 (SHIPPED)** | **816.5** | shipped-default confirmation runs: 817.4 |

The winner is two rows per workgroup of 128 with the
subgroup reduction, which is also the configuration
ggml-vulkan itself picks for K-quants on RDNA3 (`rm_kq` 2,
large workgroup, hybrid reduction): the independent tuning
converged on the reference's own answer for this silicon.
`shipped_shape` selects r2sg when the device grants
SUBGROUP and r2 (same kernel, LDS reduction) otherwise; the
shipped default passed its own `k1_check` at rel 1.267e-7
and the synthetic GPU suite on the server (3 of 3).

What 816.5 GB/s is, stated plainly: 115 percent of
llama.cpp's measured 708 GB/s, 128 percent of the 637 GB/s
trigger line, and 85 percent of the card's 960 GB/s peak,
which is the efficiency band ARCHITECTURE.md sets for
specialized kernels. One honest scope note: 708 is
llama.cpp's full-model decode rate through a serving loop;
816.5 is a K1 micro-bench over the FFN-dominated resident
set, which is exactly the Tier 2 comparison this document
prescribes (kernels benched at Glimmer shapes against
llama.cpp's number). Within that prescribed comparison the
tuned WGSL kernel beats the reference.

### The ash verdict, restated on tuned numbers

This supersedes the first landing's computed verdict above,
which stood on the untuned v2 number. Section 8's three
triggers, against the tuned K1:

1. Tuned wgpu still under 90 percent of the reference (637
   GB/s): DOES NOT FIRE. 816.5 GB/s is over the line with 28
   percent headroom, and over llama.cpp's own number by 15
   percent.
2. A capability gap blocks a required kernel: DOES NOT
   FIRE. Subgroups, SHADER_F16 and timestamps are all
   exposed and exercised; nothing K1 needed was missing.
3. A gap over 5 percent traced to Naga codegen: DOES NOT
   FIRE. There is no gap; the WGSL kernel beat the
   reference path's measured number.

**Verdict: wgpu stays the only GPU stack. The raw-Vulkan
(ash) path is not needed, no prototype is started, and the
question is closed for K1.** Section 8 stays armed as
written for the kernels that follow: K2 and K3 take the same
per-kernel comparison when they land, and a future kernel
that lands under its line after tuning reopens the ash
question for that kernel on its own numbers.

### Follow-ups from the tuning pass

- TODO T-4.2 stays open, unchanged: the full Tier 1 bench
  table (a complete forward pass) still needs a scheduled
  window with the card to itself.
- Bench-window law, amended from this night's evidence:
  record VRAM free and the co-tenant list with every matrix,
  run a stream-probe canary in the same window, and distrust
  any absolute whose canary is under roughly 100 GB/s. The
  sysfs DPM readouts on this host are not evidence.

## BACKEND-RESULTS: K2 (Q6_K) and K3 (Q5_K) (2026-10-30)

K2 and K3 landed in `crates/wgpu-compute`, following tuned
K1's structure (sixteen threads per super-block, packed scale
extraction, activation quads shared across the tile's rows,
subgroup butterfly reduction with an LDS finish and a
workgroup-memory tree fallback). `Compute::proj` and
`Compute::lm_head` now dispatch by tensor dtype through a
generalized name-keyed weight cache (Q4_K to K1, Q6_K to K2,
Q5_K to K3; a name arriving with a different dtype or geometry
refuses as an identity violation). The device binding floor
in `device.rs` rose from 128 MiB to 1 GiB, as that constant's
note always said K3 would require: the Q5_K head binds whole
at 924,571,648 bytes, and the RADV adapter grants 2 GiB.

K2 carries one layout concession, owned in its module docs:
a Q6_K super-block is 210 bytes, not a whole number of words,
so upload repacks each block into a 212-byte device stride
(210 raw bytes plus two zero pad bytes) once, at load time.
Every stream number below is computed on the RAW file bytes
(the useful stream llama.cpp's 708 is also measured on); the
device traffic is 212/210 of that. K3 needs no repack: 176
bytes is 44 whole words, and the head's 202,048 rows run
through the two-dimensional dispatch K1 proved (101,024
workgroups at the shipped shape).

**Window for everything below:** one sitting, 2026-10-30,
production Glimmer llama-server resident and untouched
(22,790,967,296 of 25,753,026,560 VRAM bytes in use, about
2.8 GiB free; `/health` returned ok before and after every
step; nothing was killed or restarted). Stream-probe canary
in the same window: 871.9 GB/s in row mode. A healthy window
by the amended bench-window law.

**Correctness (against the `gguf` crate's CPU dequantizer
plus `torch-math` matvec, the standing cross-check):**

| Check | Geometry | Result |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| K2 synthetic, 1 and 2 rows | [256 x 3] Q6_K | pass (suite) |
| K2 real, `blk.0.ffn_down.weight` | [19968 x 6656], 109,025,280 B | max rel err 6.879e-8, cosine 1.000000000, PASS (both shipped shapes) |
| K3 synthetic, 1 and 2 rows | [256 x 3] Q5_K | pass (suite) |
| K3 synthetic 2D grid | [256 x 140,000] Q5_K, 70,000 workgroups | pass (suite) |
| K3 real, `output.weight` | [6656 x 202048], 924,571,648 B | max rel err 2.433e-7, cosine 1.000000000, PASS |

**K2 bench matrix** (resident set: one `ffn_down` at
109,025,280 raw bytes plus 26 `attn_v` tensors at 1,397,760
= 145,367,040 raw bytes per iteration; 6,000 timed
iterations plus 200 warmup; median of 3 runs; `k2_bench`):

| Shape | Median GB/s | Runs |
| :--- | ---: | :--- |
| r1sg, workgroup 256 (SHIPPED) | 831.9 | 831.6, 832.4, 831.9 |
| r2sg, workgroup 256 | 826.8 | 826.8, 826.8, 827.0 |
| r1sg, workgroup 128 | 825.1 | 825.0, 825.4, 825.1 |

| r2sg, workgroup 128 (first default) | 818.6 | 818.6, 818.6, 818.5 |

The 382.0 run took 2.28 s against its siblings' 1.09 s: a
window stumble, not a shape property, recorded here and
excluded by the median. After the shipped default moved to
r1sg at workgroup 256, a confirmation triple of the shipped
configuration read 831.8, 832.2, 831.9. On Q6_K's geometry
(the wide tensor is 6,656 rows of 78 blocks) one row per
workgroup with more block-groups in flight per row beats
K1's two-rows-of-128; the shipped default follows the
evidence, per the rule stated when the shape was written.

**K3 bench matrix** (the whole head resident: 924,571,648
bytes per iteration; 2,000 timed iterations plus 200 warmup;
median of 3 runs; `k3_bench --budget-mib 1024`):

| Shape | Median GB/s | Runs |
| :--- | ---: | :--- |
| r2sg, workgroup 128 (SHIPPED, unchanged) | 813.2 | 813.8, 813.2, 813.2 |
| r4sg, workgroup 128 | 793.4 | 793.8, 793.4, 792.9 |
| r4, workgroup 128 | 791.5 | 791.6, 791.5, 791.2 |
| r2, workgroup 128 | 766.7 | 766.4, 766.9, 766.7 |
| r2sg, workgroup 256 | 761.5 | 761.6, 761.4, and a third in the same band |
| r1sg, workgroup 128 | 748.0 | 748.4, 748.0, 747.7 |
| r1, workgroup 128 | 691.1 | 690.4, 691.1, 691.1 |
| r1sg, workgroup 256 | 689.8 | 689.8, 689.2, 690.1 |

The head inverts K2's preference: at 26 blocks per row the
activation quads are re-read per workgroup row, so rows per
workgroup pay and width does not. K1's pick (two rows,
workgroup 128, subgroup) is confirmed as K3's best and the
shipped default does not move.

**Ash verdict for K2 and K3 (Section 8 applied per kernel):**
neither trigger fires for either kernel. Tuned K2 at 831.9
GB/s is 117.5 percent of llama.cpp's measured 708 and 86.7
percent of the card's 960 peak; tuned K3 at 813.2 GB/s is
114.9 percent of 708 and 84.7 percent of peak. Both sit above
the 637 line with more than 27 percent headroom, in the same
efficiency band as tuned K1 (816.5, 85 percent of peak). No
capability gap was met: the 2 GiB binding, the
two-dimensional dispatch, subgroups, and timestamps were all
exercised on the real file. No per-kernel gap above 5 percent
traces to Naga codegen; the residual distance to peak is the
same shape K1's record already analyzed. wgpu stays; no ash
prototype was started.

With K1, K2, and K3 all tuned, Glimmer's whole weight stream
now has a measured kernel: byte-share-weighted (Section 3's
77.3 / 17.1 / 5.5 split), the three medians compose to about
818 GB/s of Tier 2 micro-bench bandwidth. That is a
composition of micro-benches, stated as such; the Tier 1
full-model number remains TODO T-4.2's bar and is not claimed
here.

**Recorded for the tree, not for these kernels:** the K4 to
K8 track landed in this crate in parallel with this work
(K4 norms and residual add, K5 RoPE and KV append, K6
attention, K7 activations, K8 embedding gather and head
finish), and `Compute` now wires every step. Three defects
in that track surfaced while gating this landing and were
fixed in passing: a WGSL type error in K8's half-precision
gather (`pack2x16float` wrapped around `unpack2x16float`,
rejected by Naga on the real adapter and invisible on
adapter-less machines), a swapped residual/branch argument
pair in the K4 test's fused-mode comparison (the kernel was
right; the test composed the other order), and two lint
slips (an argument-count allowance on K4's private helper, a
digit grouping in a test seed). The full crate suite on the
server's GPU after those fixes: 40 passed, 0 failed,
including the cross-backend comparison against `cpu-compute`.

## Appendix: the adapter probe

Lives in scratch (/tmp/wgpu-probe), not in this repo: it is a
measurement tool, rerun when the stack changes. Dependencies: wgpu
27.0.1, pollster 0.4. Build on any Linux host, run on the host whose
adapters you want to see.

```rust
//! wgpu adapter probe: enumerate every adapter wgpu can see, print each
//! one's info and key limits, then print the adapter wgpu selects for a
//! HighPerformance request (the one itak-backend would get by default).
//!
//! Read-only toward the host GPU: enumeration opens the Vulkan driver
//! but dispatches no work. Intended to run on the server that hosts the
//! RX 7900 XTX (RADV), built elsewhere and copied over.

async fn run() {
    let instance = wgpu::Instance::new(&wgpu::InstanceDescriptor {
        backends: wgpu::Backends::all(),
        ..Default::default()
    });

    let adapters = instance.enumerate_adapters(wgpu::Backends::all());
    println!("enumerated_adapters: {}", adapters.len());
    for (i, adapter) in adapters.iter().enumerate() {
        let info = adapter.get_info();
        let limits = adapter.limits();
        println!(
            "[{i}] name={:?} backend={:?} device_type={:?} vendor=0x{:04x} device=0x{:04x} driver={:?} driver_info={:?}",
            info.name, info.backend, info.device_type,
            info.vendor, info.device, info.driver, info.driver_info
        );
        println!(
            "    limits: max_buffer_size={} max_storage_buffer_binding_size={} ...",
            limits.max_buffer_size, limits.max_storage_buffer_binding_size
        );
        println!(
            "    features: subgroup={} timestamp_query={} shader_f16={}",
            adapter.features().contains(wgpu::Features::SUBGROUP),
            adapter.features().contains(wgpu::Features::TIMESTAMP_QUERY),
            adapter.features().contains(wgpu::Features::SHADER_F16)
        );
    }

    let selected = instance
        .request_adapter(&wgpu::RequestAdapterOptions {
            power_preference: wgpu::PowerPreference::HighPerformance,
            compatible_surface: None,
            force_fallback_adapter: false,
        })
        .await
        .expect("request_adapter found no adapter");
    let info = selected.get_info();
    println!(
        "selected: name={:?} backend={:?} device_type={:?}",
        info.name, info.backend, info.device_type
    );
    println!("selected_limits: {:#?}", selected.limits());
}

fn main() {
    pollster::block_on(run());
}
```

# CHANGELOG: iTaK Torch Rebuild

## 2026-11-07: Second cold critic panel graded the tree DO NOT SHIP; its first fix categories landed the same day
- The panel: six cold seats over the full file inventory at 333f354, verdict DO NOT SHIP, 83 findings (0 critical, 16 high, 41 medium), the numeric core verified clean from every seat (record: the panel merge report, CRITIC-ENGINE-MERGE.md, 2026-11-07).
- Category A (snapshots): itak-kv snapshot decode refuses crafted geometry by name instead of aborting or accepting it (7a71727), and the prefix-KV seam refuses F16 KV storage by name (ca73795).
- Category D (socket seam): the platform authenticates the engine socket before dialing (owner uid and 0600 mode, mirroring the engine side) and retires desynced control connections after a timeout (07bce8a).
- Category E (platform answers): tool conversations render with their real names and calls (0578b44); cache key distinctness is pinned by field-by-field tests, unseeded sampled generations bypass the response cache, and template fetch failures are named instead of silently flattening the prompt (07fe5aa).
- Category F (proof tools): the golden and Q2/Q3 cross-check tools fail loudly: verdicts gate on the first values, failing or absent sets reach the exit code, and neither verdict tool exits 0 on a divergence (ce555fd).
- Category H (debug law): every flag-based diag seam gained an env twin in the gguf shape, the tokenizer moved onto the runtime flag, each seam gained a capture test, and the RUNBOOK gained the diagnostics switches table (a47dcf8).

- The first run failed one case, contractions: the pre-tokenizer had implemented the llama-3 split (contraction as its own piece), while llama.cpp routes `pre = llama4` to the GPT-4o pattern, where the contraction is a suffix of the word piece. `pretokenize.rs` and the crate docs now implement and document the GPT-4o pattern, with regression tests.
- Proof: crates/tokenizer/CONFORMANCE.md; harness in crates/tokenizer/examples/conformance.rs; reference in crates/tokenizer/conformance/.

# iTaK Torch rebuild: Rust engine workspace (PLAN S2, S5).
# One crate per module; the Go platform lives outside this workspace.
# These crates are the token-loop side of the seam.
#
# This root merges the per-crate versions several builders each wrote
# while scaffolding their crate (gguf, torch-math, tokenizer,
# muse-glimmer, attention): the member list is the union of crates/,
# [workspace.package] and the lint tables are restored because most
# member manifests inherit edition/license/rust-version and lints
# from here, and the release profile from the tokenizer version is
# kept.
[workspace]
resolver = "2"
members = [
    "crates/arch-llama",
    "crates/attention",
    "crates/cpu-compute",
    "crates/gguf",
    "crates/itak-engine",
    "crates/itak-kv",
    "crates/itak-loader",
    "crates/itak-spec",
    "crates/muse-glimmer",
    "crates/dflash",
    "crates/tokenizer",
    "crates/torch-math",
    "crates/wgpu-compute",
]

[workspace.package]
edition = "2021"
license = "MIT"
rust-version = "1.85"

# Lint gates are part of every module, not an afterthought: warnings
# are denied workspace-wide and clippy must run clean (David's rule,
# 2026-10-20: every module ships with debugging and lint tests built
# in from birth).
[workspace.lints.rust]
warnings = "deny"

[workspace.lints.clippy]
all = "deny"

[profile.release]
lto = "thin"

# DECISIONS: iTaK Torch Rebuild
## 2026-10-27: Models live on a dedicated NVMe drive in the server
- **Decided:** Model weights get their own NVMe drive in the server (the Kingston NV3 1 TB David bought for this purpose), mounted as the models volume. Downloads, re-downloads, and the streaming experiments all target that drive.
- **Why:** Serving loads a model once and runs it from VRAM, but the MoE streaming work reads experts constantly, and NVMe reads run roughly ten times SATA speed. The array is bulk storage and the wrong tier for hot model data. David's words: models on the NVMe is exactly why he got it.
- **Supersedes:** the array placement in the "Model weights live on the large array" decision below. The never-on-the-root-disk rule in that decision stands unchanged.
- **By:** David

## 2026-10-27: This project lives in a public repo with the full standard file set
- **Decided:** The rebuild's plan, evidence, and record are published in this repo (David2024patton/itak-torch-rebuild), public, with TODO, IDEA, PLAN, ENDGOAL, and the jump-back-in files maintained per the repo standard.
- **Why:** The benchmark record and the design work existed only in a local folder. The original engine died of exactly that failure mode: valuable work in one unpublished place. David's words: "Yes make it public. Use the GitHub skill to make the to-do etc files."
- **Supersedes:** none
- **By:** David

## 2026-10-27: The rebuild splits Go and Rust by feature, two processes, one seam
- **Decided:** Rust owns the token loop (kernels, KV caches, SSM scan, MoE streaming, speculative decoding, training compute, GPU backends). Go owns the platform (API surface, scheduling, caches, cluster, tenancy, model operations, observability, Core). Engine and platform are separate processes: control over a local socket, tokens and tensors through shared memory. Mojo remains the research lab; proven ideas graduate into the Rust crates.
- **Why:** David's standing rule is each language for the features it is best at. Go's platform code in the original is architecturally sound and gets reattached, not rewritten. The GC dividing line is the language dividing line: platform code does not care about GC pauses, the token loop does. Two processes also fix the original's FFI failure shape: the engine can restart or be replaced without the API going down.
- **Supersedes:** the original single-binary Go design with llama.cpp FFI coupling
- **By:** David (the split was proposed by Lulu on 2026-10-27 and adopted through his follow-up questions and the repo order)

## 2026-10-27: Experimental modes ship behind config flags, off by default
- **Decided:** Mamba-3 mode, cache-aware MoE routing, linear-attention swaps, and anything else unproven ship behind config flags with the default off, and earn a default only with hardware proof recorded in this repo.
- **Why:** The original Mojo engine carried a fully implemented early-exit drafting system that was dead by one boolean, and a Mamba-3 mode that never ran as shipped. Experiments that are invisible or always-on both waste the work.
- **Supersedes:** none
- **By:** David (standing build law, applied to this project 2026-10-27)

## 2026-10-27: Model weights live on the large array, never the root disk
- **Decided:** All model weights on the home server live under /mnt/alphaflux-data. Nothing model-sized goes on the root NVMe.
- **Why:** On 2026-10-27 the root disk filled, Dokploy went down, and the Glimmer test weights were deleted on David's order to recover. The storage plan (NVMe for OS, the array for bulk) only works if the weights follow it.
- **Supersedes:** the original /home/server/models placement
- **By:** David

## 2026-10-26: Vulkan is the production GPU backend on the RX 7900 XTX; ROCm is parked
- **Decided:** llama.cpp serving and all benchmark claims run on the Vulkan build. ROCm/HIP remediation (clean reinstall, likely a reset window) is David's call and is not scheduled.
- **Why:** Proven on the machine: HIP bench and CLI both wedge after model load with the GPU idle, and a 20-line HIP program fails to link against the mixed ROCm install, while Vulkan runs flawlessly on the same driver. The GPU is healthy; the ROCm userland is not.
- **Supersedes:** none
- **By:** David

## 2026-10-26: Muse Glimmer 30B serving pick is the Meta Q4_K_M build on Vulkan
- **Decided:** llama-server Vulkan, Meta Q4_K_M, context 131072, 4 slots, --jinja, f16 KV, DFlash off for shared use and on (n-max 4) solo, with reasoning_strength low injected by default at the proxy layer.
- **Why:** Measured: Q4_K_M decodes at 44.07 tok/s solo and 37.14 tok/s per user at two users; Q3 is faster but weaker, Q5 slower for marginal quality, Q6 leaves no KV room. Default reasoning strength burns the whole token budget and returns empty content; low fixes it and the answers verify correct.
- **Supersedes:** none
- **By:** Lulu, from the benchmark evidence, reported to David 2026-10-26

## 2026-10-30: The recorded Glimmer speed anchors (44.31 plain, 88.6 DFlash) are harness-relative
- **Decided:** The 2026-10-28 anchors stay in the record with their harness named, and the Section 9 sweep harness (llama-server /completion, short raw prompts, fixed 256-token generations, temperature 0) is the comparison shape for depth/operating-point claims until T-9.7 re-runs it against our own stack. On that harness: plain 41.64 tok/s, DFlash depth 4 = 103.01, depth 6 = 107.39 (the operating point by SPEC 9.4's rule), depths 8+ collapse below or near plain. Full table: bench/gpu-proof-2026-10-30.md.
- **Why:** The sweep did not reproduce the anchors within a few percent (plain -6.0%, depth 4 +16.3%, ratio 2.47x vs the recorded 2.00x), which the RUNBOOK defines as a finding, not rounding. The recorded numbers came from different shapes (llama-bench tg128 after pp512; the model-suite run), so cross-harness comparisons silently move both the rates and the ratio.
- **Supersedes:** nothing; the 2026-10-26 serving pick and its measured basis stand, with the harness caveat attached
- **By:** Lulu, from the 2026-10-30 sweep evidence, during David's approved pause window

## 2026-10-27 (historical, recorded from the failure): Shared code is published and versioned, never a relative folder
- **Decided:** Any module another module depends on is a published, versioned artifact. Relative-path replaces in module files are forbidden in this project.
- **Why:** The original iTaKCore lived only as ../Core beside the Torch tree on one machine. It was never pushed, the folder is gone, and the engine cannot be built. The measured usage surface is small (six importing files); the loss was never about size, only about the module never existing anywhere durable.
- **Supersedes:** the original go.mod replace directive pattern
- **By:** David (build law, recorded here as this project's founding lesson)

===== END FILE: DECISIONS.md =====
