1,022-token figures.

- Step 1 correctness: k23_mmq tests PASS on the card
  (bundle leg2-k23-tests); the resident_session suite
  passes with WGPU_COMPUTE_K23_MMQ=1 (bundle
  leg2-k23-resident PASS); the spec run passes IDENTITY
  and GOLDEN with the switch on. No GEMM-shaped call
  exists in a 64-token spec run, so no k23 stamp appears
  there; the stamp proof is the prefill arm below, where
  k23_q4k_mmq dispatches 2,730 times, exactly k13's
  dispatch count in the control arm. The K12 quantize
  counts are identical across arms (same totals, 9,795
  dispatches each).
- Step 2 kernel A/B (prefill_profile, diag timing, 919
  tokens): k23_q4k_mmq totals 7,942.3 ms over 2,730
  dispatches against k13_q4k_mmq's 3,694.3 ms over the
  same 2,730 dispatches in the control arm. K14, flash,
  and every other row are unchanged within noise. The
  prefill phase wall reads 10,209 ms (K23 on) against
  5,923 ms (off).
- Step 3 session wall (glimmer_generate --gpu, same
  prompt, timing off, 3 runs each): off 5,717 / 5,723 /
  5,741 (median 5,723); on 9,949 / 9,956 / 9,956
  (median 9,956). K23 costs roughly 74 percent on the
  prefill wall at this shape.
- Step 0 autopsy and step 4 no-leak: the autopsy reads
  are in the filtered single-kernel dump section below
  (the full-suite dump interleaves under parallel test
  threads); no-leak is covered by every env-unset arm in
  this session reproducing control behavior with zero
  k23 stamps (band controls, prefill off arm).

Verdict against the note's decision rule (flip only on
an autopsy improvement or a material prefill win with
correctness green): K23 is correct and decisively
SLOWER, 2.15x on its own kernel row at identical
dispatch counts. DO NOT FLIP; the switch stays off. The
llama-style staging bet loses on this card and driver,
and the loss is in the kernel itself (its per-dispatch
rates read 8.7 to 16.8 GB/s in the diag stream against
K13's roughly 46 GB/s class), not in host overhead.

### (h) step 0 autopsy, completed (filtered single-family dumps)

The full-suite dump interleaves under parallel test
threads, so the autopsy was re-read from filtered
single-thread runs (the bench/shader-autopsy.sh family
isolation pattern), cross-checked against the in-situ
dump of a live session, where the same blocks reappear
with identical numbers.

| kernel | VGPRs | spilled VGPRs | scratch | LDS |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| K13 (k12_k14 family dump, block 6) | 256 | 0 | 0 | 41,984 |
| K23 (isolated k23 dump, block 3) | 256 | 248 | 25,088 | 22,528 |

K23's staging design did what it promised on LDS
(22,528 against K13's 41,984, and exactly the note's
predicted 22,528 staged bytes), and the register
allocator paid for it: VGPRs still at the 256 cap, 248
VGPR spills and 25,088 bytes of scratch per workgroup
where K13 has none. The spill traffic is the measured
2.15x kernel loss's mechanism. Autopsy improvement on
the LDS axis alone does not change the (h) verdict.

### (i) Flash staged gates (bench/flash-rework-2026-11-06.md)

- Step 0 autopsy: the compile tests do not construct the
  staged pipeline, so the read comes from an in-situ dump
  (spec_generate_gpu with the switch on, private shader
  cache). The staged variants are the five blocks present
  in the session dump and absent from the K4-to-K8
  compile-test dump: VGPRs 60 (rule: at most 128, PASS),
  spilled VGPRs 0, scratch 0 (PASS), LDS 16,384 per
  workgroup as the driver reports it. The WGSL staging
  constant is 21,632; bench/shader-autopsy.sh's own
  header warns that in-situ LDS values differ from the
  WGSL constants by driver packing, and the 16,384 figure
  is exactly one 32x128 f32 staging block. Recorded with
  that caveat.
- Step 1 correctness: the k6_flash_staged exactness test
  passes on the card (bundle leg2-flash-exact); the
  resident_session suite passes with
  WGPU_COMPUTE_FLASH_STAGED=1 (bundle leg2-flash-resident
  PASS); spec IDENTITY and GOLDEN pass at depths 1 and 6
  with the switch on (their bundles carry the standing
  SPEED-bar FAIL artifact described at the top of this
  leg). PASS.
- Step 2 prefill A/B at 1,022 tokens (diag timing):
  k6_attn_flash totals 972.9 ms over 832 dispatches
  (control) against k6_attn_flash_staged 605.9 ms over
  832 (on): the kernel row improves 37.7 percent and
  clears the decision bar (at most 760 ms, 25 percent
  under the recorded 1,013.1) with room. Every other
  kernel row is unchanged within noise (K13 3,970.1 vs
  3,972.9; K14 1,248.0 vs 1,250.2). BUT the prefill phase
  wall moves the wrong way: 6,383 ms off against 6,558 ms
  on. Roughly 540 ms of non-kernel time appears with the
  switch on at this prompt length, against a 367 ms
  kernel saving. The decision rule requires both the row
  bar and a same-session wall improvement: at 1,022
  tokens the wall clause FAILS.
- Step 3 long context (fox prompt x820, prompt_tokens
  8,202, at or above the 8,192 the protocol demands):
  flash row 47,360.9 ms (off) against 22,820.3 ms (on),
  a 51.8 percent kernel improvement; phase wall 93,509
  ms against 66,704 ms, a 28.7 percent wall improvement.
  At long context the staged kernel wins row and wall
  together, decisively.
- Step 4 no-leak: the control arm's CSV contains zero
  k6_attn_flash_staged rows, and single-row decode never
  routes staged (no staged record appears in any
  single-row context in the session). Decode with the
  switch on (glimmer_generate --gpu, 128 tokens) reads a
  mean step of 26.04 ms (38.4 tok/s) against this
  session's plain control reading of 34.21 ms (29.2
  tok/s) from leg 1(b) and 30.01 ms (33.3 tok/s) from the
  (j) tax arm: the glimmer step clock scatters widely
  under this session's parallel CPU collection, so the
  recorded 35.5 to 35.7 band is neither reproduced nor
  refuted on that surface. On the stable surface (the
  resident spec harness's plain decode line) the session
  reads 34.08 to 34.62 tok/s across arms. The staged
  path provably does not touch single-row forwards, so
  no decode effect is attributable to it either way.

Verdict: staged flash is CORRECT everywhere and much
faster where attention dominates (long context), but at
the standard 1,022-token prefill shape the wall clause
of its own decision rule fails despite the kernel win.
DO NOT FLIP on this evidence; the flip question the
parent has to weigh is whether the long-context win
justifies a length-gated default, and where the roughly
540 ms of non-kernel time at 1,022 tokens comes from.
That host-side cost is the one open thread this leg
leaves, and it is named here rather than smoothed over.

===== FILE: bench/baseline-session-driver.py =====
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Baseline session driver (2026-11-06 consolidated card session).

Cross-backend agreement collection for Leg 1(c): the overnight
baseline pattern (5 golden prompts x 16 tokens, temperature 0,
token-id input) run against multiple stacks and compared
pairwise. The parsing and alignment mirror
bench/overnight_baseline.py exactly: llama.cpp generated ids are
[s["id"] for s in completion_probabilities]; our per-position
tops are 1-based with prefill = position 1, aligned against
llama step pos-1; a step's top-1 probability is exp(logprob) of
the sampled (greedy) token.

Subcommands:
  llama  --bin-dir D --ngl N --port P --tag T --out-dir O
         [--repo R] [--model M]
         Start llama-server from D, tokenize with D's
         llama-tokenize, complete all five prompts, write
         O/stack-llama-<tag>.json, stop the server.
  ours   --tag T --out-dir O --log pid=path [--log pid=path...]
         Parse glimmer_generate logs (CPU or --gpu path; same
         output contract) into O/stack-ours-<tag>.json.
  compare --out-dir O
         Load every stack-*.json in O, compare all pairs per
         prompt (prompt ids, generated ids position by
         position, top-1 probability deltas over the shared
         prefix), write O/compare-matrix.json and print the
         matrix.
"""

import argparse
import json
import math
import re
import subprocess
import sys
import time
import urllib.request
from pathlib import Path

PROMPT_IDS = [
    "factual_capital",
    "factual_science",
    "arithmetic_add",
    "continuation_classic",
    "code_python",
]
N_TOKENS = 16
MODEL_DEFAULT = "/mnt/models/Muse-Glimmer-30B/Muse-Glimmer-30B-KQuant-17GB-Q4_K_M.gguf"
CTX = 512
THREADS = 8


def load_prompts(repo: Path):
    by_id = {}
    for line in (repo / "golden" / "prompts.jsonl").read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines():
        if line.strip():
            rec = json.loads(line)
            by_id[rec["id"]] = rec["prompt"]
    return [(pid, by_id[pid]) for pid in PROMPT_IDS]


def step_prob(step):
    if "prob" in step:
        return step["prob"]
    return math.exp(step["logprob"])


def step_top(step):
    cands = step.get("top_probs") or step.get("top_logprobs") or []
    out = []
    for t in cands:
        p = t["prob"] if "prob" in t else math.exp(t["logprob"])
        out.append({"id": t["id"], "prob": p})
    return out


def wait_health(proc, port, log_path: Path):
    url = f"http://127.0.0.1:{port}/health"
    for _ in range(240):
        if proc.poll() is not None:
            tail = log_path.read_text(errors="replace")[-2000:]
            raise RuntimeError(f"llama-server exited early; log tail:\n{tail}")
        try:
            with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=2) as r:
                if r.status == 200:
                    return
        except Exception:
            pass
        time.sleep(0.5)
    raise RuntimeError("llama-server did not become healthy in 120 s")


def cmd_llama(a):
    bin_dir = Path(a.bin_dir)
    out_dir = Path(a.out_dir)
    out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    prompts = load_prompts(Path(a.repo))
    version = subprocess.run(
        [str(bin_dir / "llama-server"), "--version"],
        capture_output=True, text=True).stderr.strip().splitlines()
    log_path = out_dir / f"llama-server-{a.tag}.log"
    with open(log_path, "w") as lf:
        proc = subprocess.Popen(
            [str(bin_dir / "llama-server"), "-m", a.model,
             "-ngl", str(a.ngl), "-c", str(CTX), "-t", str(THREADS),
             "--host", "127.0.0.1", "--port", str(a.port)],
            stdout=lf, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT)
    result = {"stack": f"llama-{a.tag}", "bin_dir": str(bin_dir),
              "ngl": a.ngl, "version": version[-1] if version else "?",
              "prompts": {}}
    try:
        wait_health(proc, a.port, log_path)
        for pid, prompt in prompts:
            ids = json.loads(subprocess.run(
                [str(bin_dir / "llama-tokenize"), "-m", a.model, "-p", prompt,
                 "--ids", "--no-escape"],
                capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout.strip())
            body = json.dumps({
                "prompt": ids, "n_predict": N_TOKENS, "temperature": 0,
                "seed": 42, "n_probs": 5, "ignore_eos": True,
                "cache_prompt": False}).encode("utf-8")
            req = urllib.request.Request(
                f"http://127.0.0.1:{a.port}/completion", data=body,
                headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"})
            with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=1200) as r:
                resp = json.loads(r.read().decode("utf-8"))
            steps = resp["completion_probabilities"]
            result["prompts"][pid] = {
                "prompt_ids": ids,
                "generated_ids": [s["id"] for s in steps],
                "top1_probs": [step_prob(s) for s in steps],
                "first_top5": step_top(steps[0]) if steps else [],
                "raw": resp,
            }
            print(f"llama-{a.tag} {pid}: {result['prompts'][pid]['generated_ids']}",
                  flush=True)
    finally:
        proc.terminate()
        try:
            proc.wait(timeout=10)
        except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
            proc.kill()
    (out_dir / f"stack-llama-{a.tag}.json").write_text(
        json.dumps(result, ensure_ascii=False, indent=1))
    print(f"wrote stack-llama-{a.tag}.json; server stopped", flush=True)
    return 0


TOP_LINE = re.compile(
    r"^(?P<label>\w+)_top rank=(?P<rank>\d+) id=(?P<id>\d+) "
    r"tok=(?P<tok>.*) logit=(?P<logit>[-\d.]+) prob=(?P<prob>[-\d.e]+)$"
)


def parse_ours(log_text: str):
    prompt_ids = None
    generated = None
    tops = {}
    for line in log_text.splitlines():
        if line.startswith("prompt_ids="):
            prompt_ids = json.loads(line.split("=", 1)[1])
        elif line.startswith("generated_ids="):
            generated = json.loads(line.split("=", 1)[1])
        else:
            m = TOP_LINE.match(line)
            if m:
                label = m.group("label")
                pos = 1 if label == "prefill" else int(label[4:])
                tops.setdefault(pos, []).append({
                    "rank": int(m.group("rank")), "id": int(m.group("id")),
                    "logit": float(m.group("logit")),
                    "prob": float(m.group("prob"))})
    for pos in tops:
        tops[pos].sort(key=lambda r: r["rank"])
    return prompt_ids, generated, tops


def cmd_ours(a):
    out_dir = Path(a.out_dir)
    out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    result = {"stack": f"ours-{a.tag}", "prompts": {}}
    for item in a.log:
        pid, path = item.split("=", 1)
        p_ids, generated, tops = parse_ours(Path(path).read_text(errors="replace"))
        result["prompts"][pid] = {
            "prompt_ids": p_ids,
            "generated_ids": generated,
            "top1_probs": [(tops[p][0]["prob"] if tops.get(p) else None)
                           for p in range(1, N_TOKENS + 1)],
            "first_top5": [{"id": t["id"], "prob": t["prob"]}
                           for t in tops.get(1, [])],
            "tops": {str(k): v for k, v in sorted(tops.items())},
        }
        print(f"ours-{a.tag} {pid}: {generated}", flush=True)
    (out_dir / f"stack-ours-{a.tag}.json").write_text(
        json.dumps(result, ensure_ascii=False, indent=1))
    print(f"wrote stack-ours-{a.tag}.json", flush=True)
    return 0


def cmd_compare(a):
    out_dir = Path(a.out_dir)
    stacks = {}
    for f in sorted(out_dir.glob("stack-*.json")):
        d = json.loads(f.read_text())
        stacks[d["stack"]] = d
    names = sorted(stacks)
    matrix = {"stacks": names, "pairs": {}}
    print(f"stacks: {names}")
    for i, x in enumerate(names):
        for y in names[i + 1:]:
            pair = {"prompts": {}, "any_token_divergence": False,
                    "max_abs_top1_delta": 0.0}
            for pid in PROMPT_IDS:
                px = stacks[x]["prompts"].get(pid, {})
                py = stacks[y]["prompts"].get(pid, {})
                gx = px.get("generated_ids") or []
                gy = py.get("generated_ids") or []
                prefix = 0
                for u, v in zip(gx, gy):
                    if u != v:
                        break
                    prefix += 1
                first_div = None
                if prefix < min(len(gx), len(gy)):
                    first_div = prefix + 1
                deltas = []
                for pos in range(prefix):
                    ax = (px.get("top1_probs") or [None] * 16)[pos]
                    ay = (py.get("top1_probs") or [None] * 16)[pos]
                    if ax is not None and ay is not None:
                        deltas.append(ax - ay)
                md = max((abs(d) for d in deltas), default=0.0)
                pair["max_abs_top1_delta"] = max(pair["max_abs_top1_delta"], md)
                if first_div is not None:
                    pair["any_token_divergence"] = True
                pair["prompts"][pid] = {
                    "prompt_ids_match": px.get("prompt_ids") == py.get("prompt_ids"),
                    "generated_x": gx, "generated_y": gy,
                    "prefix_agreement": prefix,
                    "first_divergence_pos": first_div,
                    "top1_deltas_shared_prefix": deltas,
                    "max_abs_top1_delta": md,
                }
                print(f"{x} vs {y} {pid}: prefix={prefix} "
                      f"first_div={first_div} max|delta|={md:.4f}")
            matrix["pairs"][f"{x} vs {y}"] = pair
    (out_dir / "compare-matrix.json").write_text(
        json.dumps(matrix, ensure_ascii=False, indent=1))
    print("wrote compare-matrix.json", flush=True)
    return 0


def main():
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    sub = p.add_subparsers(dest="cmd", required=True)
    q = sub.add_parser("llama")
    q.add_argument("--bin-dir", required=True)
    q.add_argument("--ngl", type=int, required=True)
    q.add_argument("--port", type=int, required=True)
    q.add_argument("--tag", required=True)
    q.add_argument("--out-dir", required=True)
    q.add_argument("--repo", default=".")
    q.add_argument("--model", default=MODEL_DEFAULT)
    q.set_defaults(fn=cmd_llama)
    q = sub.add_parser("ours")
    q.add_argument("--tag", required=True)
    q.add_argument("--out-dir", required=True)
    q.add_argument("--log", action="append", required=True)
    q.set_defaults(fn=cmd_ours)
    q = sub.add_parser("compare")
    q.add_argument("--out-dir", required=True)
    q.set_defaults(fn=cmd_compare)
    a = p.parse_args()
    return a.fn(a)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

===== END FILE: bench/baseline-session-driver.py =====

===== FILE: bench/bench-phase-a.sh =====
#!/bin/bash
# Phase A: llama-bench speed + VRAM, Vulkan vs HIP/ROCm x Q3/Q4/Q5/Q6
# Run on ubuntu-server after Glimmer downloads finish. Sequential, logs to /tmp/bench-results/
set -u
OUT=/tmp/bench-results
mkdir -p "$OUT"
MODELS_DIR=/home/server/models/muse-glimmer
declare -A MODELS=(
  [Q3_K_XL]="$MODELS_DIR/Muse-Glimmer-30B-UD-Q3_K_XL.gguf"
  [Q4_K_M]="$MODELS_DIR/meta/Muse-Glimmer-30B-KQuant-17GB-Q4_K_M.gguf"
  [Q5_K_M]="$MODELS_DIR/Muse-Glimmer-30B-UD-Q5_K_M.gguf"
  [Q6_K_XL]="$MODELS_DIR/Muse-Glimmer-30B-UD-Q6_K_XL.gguf"
)
declare -A BACKENDS=(
  [vulkan]=/home/server/llama.cpp/build-vulkan/bin/llama-bench
  [rocm]=/home/server/llama.cpp/build-rocm/bin/llama-bench
)
vram_used() { cat /sys/class/drm/card*/device/mem_info_vram_used 2>/dev/null | sort -n | tail -1; }
for b in vulkan rocm; do
  for q in Q3_K_XL Q4_K_M Q5_K_M Q6_K_XL; do
    m="${MODELS[$q]}"; bin="${BACKENDS[$b]}"
    [ -f "$m" ] || { echo "SKIP $b $q missing model" >> "$OUT/summary.txt"; continue; }
    log="$OUT/bench_${b}_${q}.log"
    peak="$OUT/vram_${b}_${q}.txt"
    echo "=== $b $q $(date -Is) ===" | tee -a "$OUT/summary.txt"
    ( max=0; while true; do v=$(vram_used); [ -n "$v" ] && [ "$v" -gt "$max" ] && max=$v; echo "$max" > "$peak"; sleep 2; done ) &
    SAMPLER=$!
    "$bin" -m "$m" -ngl 999 -p 512 -n 128 -r 3 > "$log" 2>&1
    echo "BENCH_EXIT:$?" >> "$log"
    kill $SAMPLER 2>/dev/null; wait $SAMPLER 2>/dev/null
    grep -E "llama-bench|error|failed" "$log" | tail -4 >> "$OUT/summary.txt" || true
    echo "peak_vram_bytes: $(cat "$peak" 2>/dev/null)" >> "$OUT/summary.txt"
  done
done
echo "PHASE_A_DONE" >> "$OUT/summary.txt"

===== END FILE: bench/bench-phase-a.sh =====

===== FILE: bench/bench-phase-b.sh =====
#!/bin/bash
# Phase B: llama-server accuracy + reasoning_strength + 2-user concurrency + KV log capture
# Usage: bench-phase-b.sh <backend: vulkan|rocm> <model gguf path> <tag>
# Server on port 18090, -c 131072 -np 4 (shared profile from research). Logs to /tmp/bench-results/
set -u
BACKEND="${1:?backend}"; MODEL="${2:?model}"; TAG="${3:?tag}"
OUT=/tmp/bench-results; mkdir -p "$OUT"
BIN=/home/server/llama.cpp/build-${BACKEND}/bin/llama-server
[ "$BACKEND" = "rocm" ] && BIN=/home/server/llama.cpp/build-rocm/bin/llama-server
SLOG="$OUT/server_${BACKEND}_${TAG}.log"
"$BIN" -m "$MODEL" -ngl 99 -c 131072 -np 4 --jinja --host 127.0.0.1 --port 18090 > "$SLOG" 2>&1 &
SRV=$!
for _ in $(seq 1 60); do curl -s -o /dev/null http://127.0.0.1:18090/health && break; sleep 5; done
grep -iE "kv|buffer" "$SLOG" | head -20 > "$OUT/kvlog_${BACKEND}_${TAG}.txt" || true
python3 - "$OUT" "$TAG" "$BACKEND" <<'PYEOF'
import json, sys, time, urllib.request, concurrent.futures
out, tag, backend = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3]
URL = "http://127.0.0.1:18090/v1/chat/completions"
PROMPTS = [
 ("math", "A store sells pencils in packs of 6 for $4.50 per pack. Maria needs 84 pencils and has a coupon for 15% off her total. How much does she pay? Show your work step by step, then give the final amount."),
 ("go_code", "Write a Go function `MedianOfTwoSortedArrays(a, b []int) float64` that returns the median of two sorted slices in O(log(min(n,m))) time. Code only, no explanation."),
 ("logic", "Three boxes are labeled 'Apples', 'Oranges', and 'Apples & Oranges', but every label is wrong. You may draw one fruit from one box. Which box do you draw from, and how do you then correctly label all three? Answer concisely."),
 ("json", "Extract the data and reply with ONLY a JSON object, no other text: 'Jane Cooper, age 34, ordered 3 units of SKU-2214 on March 3rd, 2026, total $129.99, shipping to Austin, TX.' Keys: name, age, units, sku, date (ISO format), total, city, state."),
 ("factual", "In Ursula K. Le Guin's novel The Left Hand of Darkness, what is the name of the planet where most of the story takes place, what are its people called, and what is unusual about their biology? Two or three sentences."),
 ("summary", "Summarize in exactly 3 bullet points: Continuous batching lets an inference server swap finished requests out and new ones in at every token step instead of waiting for a whole batch. This raises GPU utilization because short requests no longer idle behind long ones. The cost is scheduler complexity and the need for paged KV cache management so sequences can start and stop without fragmenting memory. Operators also gain per-request controls like max tokens and stop sequences, which batch-at-once systems handle poorly."),
]
def ask(prompt, extra=None):
    body = {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}], "temperature": 0, "max_tokens": 512}
    if extra: body.update(extra)
    req = urllib.request.Request(URL, data=json.dumps(body).encode(), headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"})
    t0 = time.time()
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=900) as r:
        d = json.load(r)
    dt = time.time() - t0
    return d["choices"][0]["message"]["content"], d.get("usage", {}), dt
res = {"backend": backend, "tag": tag, "accuracy": {}, "reasoning": {}, "concurrency": {}}
for name, p in PROMPTS:
    c, u, dt = ask(p)
    res["accuracy"][name] = {"content": c, "usage": u, "seconds": round(dt, 2)}
# reasoning_strength low vs unset(default) on the math prompt
c, u, dt = ask(PROMPTS[0][1], {"chat_template_kwargs": {"reasoning_strength": "low"}})
res["reasoning"]["low"] = {"usage": u, "seconds": round(dt, 2), "content": c}
res["reasoning"]["default_usage"] = res["accuracy"]["math"]["usage"]
# 2-user concurrency: long generation from both at once
LONG = "Write a detailed explanation of how a sourdough starter works, covering the microbiology, feeding schedule, troubleshooting, and how to use it in a basic loaf recipe."
def worker(i):
    return ask(LONG)
with concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2) as ex:
    t0 = time.time(); futs = [ex.submit(worker, i) for i in range(2)]
    outs = [f.result() for f in futs]; wall = time.time() - t0
per = []
for c, u, dt in outs:
    ct = u.get("completion_tokens", 0)
    per.append({"completion_tokens": ct, "seconds": round(dt, 2), "tok_per_s": round(ct / dt, 2) if dt else 0})
res["concurrency"] = {"wall_seconds": round(wall, 2), "per_user": per,
                      "aggregate_tok_per_s": round(sum(u.get("completion_tokens", 0) for _, u, _ in outs) / wall, 2)}
with open(f"{out}/phaseb_{backend}_{tag}.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(res, f, indent=1)
print("PHASE_B_DONE", backend, tag)
PYEOF
kill $SRV 2>/dev/null; wait $SRV 2>/dev/null
echo "PHASE_B_${BACKEND}_${TAG}_DONE"

===== FILE: bench/calibrator-evidence-2026-11-07.md =====
# Calibrator evidence: the batch-1 artifact and the missing per-row numbers (2026-11-07)

Lane: `lane/calibrator-evidence`, based on main
0ecdc8ff5efc3da0d00b5806c8f2796b65096132. VM-side build
and gates only; no card run in this lane, and the
shipped band table is NOT changed by it (see the last
section).

## The defects, from the wave19 record

The wave19 card session (bench/wave19-session-2026-11-07.md)
ran `calibrate_profile` on the RX 7900 XTX and proved
the auto-tune profile end to end, but its derived table
exposed two defects in the calibrator itself:

1. **Batch-1 artifact rows.** Three derived cells
   (q4k attn, q4k kv, q5k ffn) included batch 1 as an
   MMV win. It cannot be one: the calibration's MMV arm
   pins its band cells to `2-16`, so at batch 1 the
   routing ladder dispatches the plain GEMV form in
   BOTH arms. The session's diag census is unambiguous:
   50 batch-1 GEMV dispatches per shape (25 per arm)
   and zero MMV dispatches at batch 1. The sub-0.98x
   median the old derivation read as a win is
   inter-arm drift between two runs of the same form.
   The old rule asked only about timing and agreement;
   it never asked whether the MMV form dispatched.

   The artifact was cosmetically harmless to routing
   (the band parser clamps derived cells to the
   kernels' 2..=16 band, so a cell text like "1-12"
   routed exactly "2-12"), but it falsified the
   evidence: the derived table claimed a measurement
   that never happened, and any cell-by-cell comparison
   against the shipped table counted a phantom
   difference at row 1.

2. **No per-cell evidence.** The calibrator printed
   only the derived table: nine cell strings, no
   medians, no ratios. A cell that differed from the
   shipped table could not be checked against the
   numbers that produced it without mining the diag
   stream, and the session showed the diag stream does
   not reproduce the derivation (it records dispatches,
   not the two arms' per-row medians). A calibration
   whose cells cannot be checked from its own output
   is weak evidence, and the wave19 comparison had to
   be argued from the census rather than read off the
   run.

## The fix: exclusion by construction

The rule "a row the MMV form cannot dispatch is never
a win" now lives in the shared derivation helpers in
`crates/wgpu-compute/src/profile.rs`, so every caller
of the derivation inherits it, not only the example
that prints the table:

- `mmv_can_dispatch(rows)`: the kernels' own band,
  `MMV_MIN_BATCH..=MMV_MAX_BATCH` (2..=16), imported
  from the K19 module that defines it. This is the
  same band the routing layer enforces
  (`parse_mmv_band` clamps cells to it;
  `MmvBands::routes` floors at its low end), so the
  derivation and the router now read dispatchability
  from one ground truth.
- `mmv_row_win(rows, mmv_ms, control_ms, agrees)`:
  the whole derivation rule in one predicate:
  dispatchable AND both arms agree with the direct
  GEMV form AND `mmv_wins` (the unchanged 0.98x timing
  rule). The calibrator derives its cells and its
  evidence verdicts from this one predicate, so the
  printed evidence and the derived table cannot
  disagree about a row.
- `derive_band_ranges` enforces the same exclusion at
  the grouping step: a win flag at an undispatchable
  row never joins a range, even when a caller hands in
  raw timing verdicts. An excluded row also does not
  bridge two runs (a win at row 1 next to a loss at
  row 2 does not pull a row-3 win into a span starting
  earlier). This is the same rule at the one pinch
  point every derivation passes through, not a second
  rule and not a filter over the printed table.

Unchanged, deliberately: the 0.98x win rule
(`mmv_wins` and `MMV_WIN_RATIO`), the band semantics,
the profile format's key=value lines, the resolution
precedence, the ceiling derivation, and the
calibrator's refusal behavior.

### Pins

New unit tests in profile.rs:

- `mmv_dispatch_band_edges`: 0 and 1 cannot dispatch;
  2 and 16 can; 17 cannot.
- `batch_one_timing_win_never_enters_a_derived_cell`:
  the artifact as a synthetic cell set. Raw timing
  wins at rows 1-4 derive "2-4"; a batch-1 win alone
  derives the closed cell "1"; wins at 1 and 3 with a
  loss at 2 derive "3" (no bridging); and the composed
  predicate refuses the same batch-1 numbers it would
  accept at row 2.
- `evidence_lines_carry_the_row_numbers_and_verdict`
  and `profile_with_evidence_comments_loads_identically`:
  below.

Foundation pins kept green: the shipped-derivation
win-rule pin and the shipped-table derivation shapes
("2,4-12" from the committed sweep's win pattern) are
unchanged. One existing assertion WAS adjusted, and it
is the one the brief allows: the all-verdicts-true
sweep case asserted the derived cell "1-16", but the
sweep's row-1 entry is exactly the artifact position;
with the exclusion, an all-wins sweep derives "2-16".
The other assertions in that test never marked row 1
as a win and did not move.

## The evidence format

`RowEvidence` (family, shape, rows, control median,
MMV median, agreement) renders one line per measured
row, in a stable greppable format:

```
evidence family=q4k shape=attn rows=1 control_ms=1.0000 mmv_ms=0.9000 ratio=0.900 agree=yes verdict=excluded
evidence family=q4k shape=attn rows=6 control_ms=1.0000 mmv_ms=0.8000 ratio=0.800 agree=yes verdict=win
```

- `ratio` is the MMV median over the control median,
  three decimals; `n/a` when the control median is not
  positive (no measurement, per `mmv_wins`).
- `verdict` is `win` (the row enters the derived
  cell), `no-win` (measured and dispatchable, but the
  timing or the agreement failed), or `excluded` (the
  form cannot dispatch at this row; the ratio is
  printed anyway, so the exclusion itself is
  auditable rather than silent).

The calibrator prints all 99 lines (9 cells x 11 rows)
after the two arms and BEFORE the derived table, under
a header naming the predicate, so the table reads as
the conclusion of the evidence. It then writes the
same lines into the profile file as `#` comments via
`write_profile_with_evidence` /
`CalibrationProfile::render_with_evidence`, between
the header comment and the key=value lines. The
format's key=value lines are byte-identical to the
bare render, and the parser already skips comments;
the round-trip pin proves a written evidence-bearing
profile loads back `Loaded` with identical cells,
ceiling, and adapter key, and that the file on disk
still carries the comments.

## What this lane did not do

- **The shipped table is not changed.** The wave19
  derived table also differed from the shipped table
  in five cells on dispatchable rows; those are real
  measurements to weigh, not artifacts to erase. A
  re-derivation with the evidence printed, judged cell
  by cell with the per-row numbers beside it, is a
  future card run's job. This lane only makes that
  future run produce auditable output and artifact-free
  cells.
- No card run: the calibrator's card behavior is
  exercised by the same future run. The refusal paths
  were re-demonstrated here on the adapterless VM
  (below).

## Verification (this VM, no adapter)

- `cargo test -p wgpu-compute -p dflash -p itak-spec`:
  354 passed, 0 failed across 32 test binaries; the
  profile module is 13/13 (9 foundation tests, 4 new).
- `cargo clippy -p wgpu-compute --all-targets -- -D warnings`:
  clean.
- `cargo fmt --check`: clean.
- `cargo check --workspace`: clean.
- Refusal path 1 (reps floor):
  `calibrate_profile --out /tmp/cal-refusal-out.txt --reps 5`
  prints `REFUSED: reps 5 is below the 20-repetition
  verdict floor; ... nothing written`, exits 1, and the
  output file does not exist afterward.
- Refusal path 2 (no adapter): `calibrate_profile
  --out /tmp/cal-refusal-out2.txt` at default reps
  prints `REFUSED: no suitable GPU on this machine to
  calibrate (arm control; enumerated: []); nothing
  written`, exits 1, writes nothing (no file at the
  `--out` path, no default profile directory created).
  Both refusals behave exactly as on the base commit:
  the refusal code precedes the derivation in `run()`
  and was not touched.

===== END FILE: bench/calibrator-evidence-2026-11-07.md =====

===== FILE: bench/chat-template-tools-2026-11-07.md =====
# Chat template tool conversations (2026-11-07)

Lane `lane/chat-template-tools`, from main 2a2030e.
Two HIGH findings from the cold critic panel
(`~/workspace/reports/critic-engine-2026-11-07/CRITIC-ENGINE-MERGE.md`,
Category E), both executed by the Mop-up seat against the model's own
ATEM template (`platform/internal/chattemplate/testdata/glimmer-atem.jinja`).

## Finding 1 (HIGH): tool messages silently flattened to an empty name

`chattemplate.Message` carried only `Role` and `Content`, and `Render`
built each message dict with only those two keys. The fixture's tool
branch looks up `message.get('name')`, falls back to a `tool_call_id`
search over `tool_calls` — neither could exist — and ended with an
empty name.

### Before evidence

Executed probe on the base tree (a temporary test through the real
`Render`, since removed): a bare tool message rendered, with no error,

```
<|start|>tool <|message|><tool_output name="">
result-42
</tool_output></tool_output><|eot|>
```

Assistant messages lost the same way in the other direction: with no
`tool_calls` key representable, a tool-calling turn rendered as a
plain text turn. This contradicted the package's own contract
("never a silently flattened prompt").

### Fix

`Message` now carries every field the fixture's message branches
read, and only those:

| Message field | Template reads it as | Where the fixture reads it |
|---|---|---|
| `Name` | `name` | tool branch, `message.get('name')` |
| `ToolCallID` | `tool_call_id` | tool branch fallback lookup |
| `ToolCalls []ToolCall` | `tool_calls` | tool branch scan; assistant branch |
| `ReasoningContent` | `reasoning_content` | assistant branch |
| `Recipient` | `recipient` | assistant branch |
| `EndTurn *bool` | `end_turn` | assistant branch |

`ToolCall` carries `ID`, `Type`, and `Function` (`FunctionCall`:
`Name`, `Arguments map[string]any`). The template refuses a call
whose arguments are not a mapping, so arguments are structured data,
never a JSON string.

Message dicts bind keys in a fixed authored order (role, content,
then the optional fields in the order above), and optional fields
are ABSENT when unset rather than present-but-empty, so
`message.get('name')` answers none for a plain message exactly as
the reference environment does.

Name resolution: `Render` resolves every tool message's name before
rendering — the explicit `Name`, else the function name of the tool
call whose id equals the message's `ToolCallID` (the same lookup the
template itself performs) — and refuses the render with the new
`ErrUnresolvableTool` when neither yields a name. The refusal is
deliberately template-independent: a name the ATEM protocol prompt
would print empty is a malformed conversation for this platform,
whatever template is configured, and the server maps it to the same
named `chat_template_error` (502) as every other render refusal.
That is the panel's prescribed shape ("refuse an unresolvable tool
message by name") taken at the package boundary rather than the API
boundary, so no caller of `Render` can flatten one either.

Two existing tests met the new contract and were adjusted with the
reason recorded in place: `TestRoleConditionalsWithElifAndElse`'s
tool message now carries a name (its branch does not read it), and
`TestUntakenBranchIsNotEvaluated`'s taken-branch tool message
carries a name so the render reaches the branch it tests (a nameless
one now refuses earlier, with `ErrUnresolvableTool`).

## Finding 2 (HIGH): the template's `tojson` refused; tool paths unreachable

The fixture calls `| tojson` at L43 and throughout the tool
definitions macro (L68, L73). The renderer implemented four filters
and refused `tojson` by name (pinned by a test); `Render` bound no
`tools` value, so `{% if tools %}` was always falsy and the tool
paths never evaluated. The golden test that "renders the real
template whole" covered only tool-less conversations.

### Before evidence

Executed probe on the base tree: `{{ 'x' | tojson }}` returned
`chattemplate: unsupported construct: filter "tojson"`.

### Fix

- `evalFilter` gains `tojson` (`evalToJSON` in render.go), with
  Jinja's semantics for the shapes involved:
  - Default form is Python `json.dumps` compact output: separators
    `,` and `:` with no spaces, mapping keys SORTED (Jinja's
    `sort_keys` defaults to true — the ATEM schema dump's key order
    depends on it), integral floats without a fraction, `true` /
    `false` / `null`, NaN and infinities as Python's bare tokens.
  - String escaping follows the plain `json.dumps` form for the
    quote (`\"`), backslash, control characters (short escapes for
    `\n \r \t \b \f`, else `\u00XX`), non-ASCII as `\uXXXX` with
    UTF-16 surrogate pairs above the BMP (ensure_ascii), and the
    HTML-safe escapes for `<`, `>`, `&` (`\u003c` etc.).
    Named divergence: Jinja's own `tojson` additionally unicode-
    escapes `"` and `'` in its HTML-safe pass. This renderer
    follows the plain form for the quote because the fixture's
    schema dumps are produced, in the reference stack, by
    llama.cpp's minja runtime, whose `tojson` is a plain
    nlohmann::json dump; the golden tests byte-compare against
    that form. The `'` escape is not applied by either form the
    fixture can reach (plain dumps never escape it; minja does
    not), so it is not applied.
  - Keywords: `indent` (non-negative integer) switches to the
    pretty form (`, ` after colons... precisely: `": "` after keys,
    one entry per line, padded by level) and `sort_keys=false`
    keeps recorded insertion order. The parser previously refused
    ALL filter keyword arguments; it now carries them for `tojson`
    only, and every other filter still refuses them by name.
    Positional arguments, a boolean `indent`, unknown keywords,
    and `tojson` over an undefined or builtin value refuse by name.
  - Nesting is depth-capped (512) with a named refusal, and the
    encoded output charges the render's output budget, like
    `replace` and `join` already do.
- `Params.Tools []Tool` binds the `tools` value
  (`Tool{Type, Function ToolFunction{Name, Description,
  Parameters map[string]any}}`). A definition with an empty `Type`
  binds as the function object itself, matching how the template
  unwraps either shape. When no tools are given the name stays
  UNDEFINED (not an empty list), so `tools is defined` and
  `{% if tools %}` answer exactly as before for tool-less requests.
- The test that pinned the `tojson` refusal is replaced by
  `TestToJSONFilter` (eleven pinned encodings) and
  `TestToJSONFilterRefusals` (five named refusals).
- The coverage claim is corrected in both places it was made (the
  extended-subset section header and the user-only golden's
  comment), and the golden coverage is extended, below.

### Two latent bugs the tool paths exposed once they could run

Both were invisible while the paths were unreachable; both are in
this lane because the golden below cannot render without them.

1. **String + filtered value.** The fixture's recipients line is
   `'# Valid recipients: ' + rns.recipients | join(', ') + '.'`.
   Jinja binds the filter tighter than `+`; this parser's `add`
   operand is a whole conditional expression, so the filter node
   landed as the tree top and the left add evaluated to undefined,
   refusing. The `add` evaluation now completes exactly that shape:
   when the right operand's evaluated value is undefined AND its
   tree root is a bare filter application over a name/attribute/
   index chain, that filter node is evaluated. This is sound
   because filters are pure. The deeper parse difference stays:
   a filter whose BASE is itself the concatenation still refuses
   by name, and no shipped shape uses it. Pinned indirectly by
   both pre-existing goldens (the user-only and system goldens
   carry the same recipients line and pass unchanged).
2. **Empty mapping literal.** `{'a': {}}` cannot tokenize: the
   template tokenizer cuts a tag at the first `}}`, which is the
   literal's own close followed by the tag's. Real Jinja lexes
   strings and nesting; this bounded tokenizer does not, and the
   gap is pre-existing for every construct, not specific to this
   lane. The lane's nested-literal test case was rewritten to a
   non-empty inner mapping rather than reworking the tokenizer.

## The dict.items() ordering MEDIUM, and the decision

The panel's MEDIUM (render.go, Category E): `dict.items()` iterated
in sorted-key order while Jinja iterates insertion order, and the
ATEM renderer prints one parameter block per pair, so the order IS
prompt text. The panel notes it "lands the moment that gap is
fixed" — this lane is that moment.

Decision: CARRY INSERTION ORDER; the change was contained.

- `value` gains a `keys []string` field: the iteration order of a
  dict's keys, nil meaning "no recorded order, iterate sorted"
  (dict literals, `namespace()` state — orders authored in the
  template or accumulated as state, which keep their historical
  sorted iteration; templates like the fixture's keep their named
  state in lists anyway).
- A new `orderedDict` constructor records order; message dicts,
  tool-call dicts, tool definitions, and JSON-converted data use
  it. `items()` iterates `orderedKeys()`; `{% set ns.attr %}` on
  an ordered dict appends a genuinely new key to its order (with a
  scope write-back for the grown slice), matching Python dict
  assignment.
- `tojson` with `sort_keys=false` likewise emits recorded order;
  the default still sorts, so ATEM schema dumps are unaffected.

The one order this lane does NOT restore is the HTTP wire order of
`arguments` / `parameters` objects: the API layer decodes them into
`map[string]any`, and `encoding/json` has already discarded key
order before conversion runs. The converter therefore records
sorted order for decoded maps. Consequences, stated plainly:

- Tool DEFINITIONS are unaffected: the fixture serializes them
  through `tojson`, whose default sorts keys, exactly Jinja's
  default. Byte-identical either way.
- Tool CALL arguments print through `items()`, so over the HTTP
  path they print in sorted key order, where a reference Jinja
  render of the same request JSON would print wire order. The
  ATEM protocol parses parameter blocks by name, so this is a
  prompt-text difference, not a protocol difference, but it is a
  real one and it is named here rather than papered over: the
  golden test's argument expectations (`city` before `days`) are
  the sorted order the shipped path produces, and they would hold
  in Jinja only for a request whose wire order was also sorted.
- Restoring wire order end to end requires decoding chat requests
  with an order-preserving JSON decoder and carrying that order
  through the API types. That is a server-layer change with its
  own blast radius (the cache key marshals the request struct);
  it is the immediate follow-up this lane makes reachable, and it
  is deliberately NOT half-done here.

A caller building `Arguments`/`Parameters` in Go code (the
`chattemplate` package used directly) gets true insertion order
only in the sense above: a Go map literal has no order to give, so
direct callers who care must also accept sorted as the recorded
order today. The value model itself is no longer the blocker.

## Field flow, HTTP layer to template

The API types had no place for these fields; they do now.

- `chatRequest` gains `Tools []chatTool` (`"tools"`).
  `chatTool{type, function{name, description, parameters}}`;
  `parameters` decodes into `map[string]any`.
- `chatMessage` gains `name`, `tool_call_id`, `tool_calls`
  (`[]chatToolCall{id, type, function{name, arguments}}`),
  `reasoning_content`, `recipient`, `end_turn` (`*bool`).
- `buildPrompt` now takes the whole `*chatRequest` and converts:
  `convertMessage` maps each wire message field for field into
  `chattemplate.Message` (including each call's id/type/name/
  arguments), and tools map into `chattemplate.Tool` for
  `Params.Tools`.
- `validateChat` relaxes one rule for the new shape: an assistant
  message carrying `tool_calls` may have empty `content` (a pure
  tool-calling turn); content is still required for every other
  message.
- Nothing else in the request path changed: the response cache
  key still marshals the whole request struct, so requests that
  differ in tools or tool calls key differently with no extra
  work (the cache findings themselves belong to a separate lane).

End-to-end pin: `TestChatWithToolsRendersToolNames` posts a full
tool request over HTTP through a configured ATEM-shaped template
and asserts the engine receives the definitions block (through
`tojson`), the call, and the tool output under the name resolved
from `tool_call_id`; `TestChatUnresolvableToolMessageIsNamed`
asserts the orphan tool message returns 502 `chat_template_error`.

## After evidence

New and extended tests (all passing; the failing-before captures
are the executed probes quoted above):

- `TestToJSONFilter` — 11 encodings, including the HTML-safe
  escapes, sorted mapping keys, nesting, and both indent forms.
- `TestToJSONFilterRefusals` — positional indent, boolean indent,
  unknown kwarg, builtin, undefined: all `ErrUnsupported`.
- `TestGlimmerToolMessageWithName` — explicit name renders.
- `TestGlimmerToolMessageResolvedByCallID` — id-resolved name
  renders, and the assistant call renders its arguments.
- `TestGlimmerToolMessageUnresolvableRefuses` — orphan tool
  message returns `ErrUnresolvableTool`.
- `TestGlimmerATEMTemplateWithTools` — the end-to-end golden:
  one tool definition (metadata line through `tojson`, schema
  line with sorted nested keys), user turn, tool call (ATEM form,
  argument blocks in sorted order as recorded above), tool result
  under its resolved name, plain assistant reply, generation
  prompt. Byte-exact.
- The two pre-existing Glimmer goldens and the full pre-existing
  suite pass unchanged apart from the two test adjustments
  recorded under Finding 1 and the removed `tojson` refusal pin.

- `cargo check --workspace` from the repo root — clean; the Rust
  tree is untouched by this lane.

## Deliberately left

  the HTTP decode (named above as the follow-up this lane makes

===== FILE: bench/chunked-gemv-2026-11-05.md =====
# Chunked GEMV arm: the dispatch-shape control for the small-batch chase (2026-11-05)

Branch `lane/chunked-gemv`, from main `88cb83a`. VM gates only in this
note; the speed verdict is the server head-to-head protocol at the end.

## Why this arm exists

The streaming-rate research (2026-11-04) carries the strix-llama.cpp
RADV finding: through a shared-weight small-batch path, batches 3, 5,
and 6 ran several times slower than 1, 2, and 4, and the fork's fix
was splitting a batch into scaling (power-of-two) column counts. Our
own K18 shared-weight product shows the same band shape problem (it
streams at a fraction of GEMV's rate). Two explanations are live:

1. The shared-weight kernel shape itself is the problem on RADV.
2. The dispatch shape is the problem: one dispatch at an arbitrary
   row count in the 2..15 band schedules badly, whatever the kernel.

The MMV register-streaming prototype (lane/mmv-prototype) tests a new
kernel. This arm tests explanation 2 with no new kernel at all: it
serves the same batch through the shipped GEMV kernels, split into
dispatches whose row counts are all powers of two. If chunked GEMV
recovers the band, the win was dispatch shape and the cheap fix
ships. If it does not, the kernel shape is convicted and MMV (or its
successor) is the road. Either result decides something; that is the
point of a control arm.

## The strategy

In `prepare_proj` (crates/wgpu-compute/src/session.rs), the single
routing point for plain projections, a new rung sits between the K18
small-batch rung and the whole-batch GEMV fallback, for all three
quant families (Q4_K via K1, Q6_K via K2, Q5_K via K3):

- Band: batch in 2..=WGPU_COMPUTE_CHUNKED_GEMV_MAX_ROWS and below
  GEMM_MIN_ROWS (16). The env resolves exactly like the K18
  threshold (compute.rs, `resolve_chunked_gemv_max_rows`); the
  shipped default is 1, which is OFF, so the ladder is byte-for-byte
  the shipped ladder until a proof moves the value.
- Decomposition (`pow2_chunks`, unit-gated): greedy largest
  power-of-two first. 7 becomes rows [4, 2, 1] at starts [0, 4, 6];
  a power-of-two batch stays one dispatch.
- Each chunk is prepared by the kernel's new `prepare_rows`: the
  SAME pipeline and the SAME shader, with bindings 1 (input) and 2
  (output) bound as buffer windows (`wgpu::BufferBinding` with
  offset and size) over rows `start..start+len` of the resident
  buffers, so the kernel sees the window as its whole batch. The
  weights binding stays whole; the params block carries the chunk's
  row count. `prepare_inner` gained an optional window parameter;
  with no window it binds exactly as before (`as_entire_binding`),
  so every existing prepare path is untouched. Shaders are
  byte-identical: no WGSL changed anywhere in this arm.
- Window validation is shared (`resolve_row_window` in
  k1_q4k_gemv.rs, used by all three kernels): an empty window, a
  window past either buffer, or a window offset that is not a
  multiple of the device's `min_storage_buffer_offset_alignment`
  refuses with a named `WgpuError::InvalidTensor`. The session's
  `try_chunked_*` composition catches a refusal at plan time, logs
  it by name through the diag channel, and returns None, so the
  whole-batch GEMV form serves that projection. Composition never
  substitutes inside a dispatch.
- Alignment reachability, stated plainly: a window at row r needs
  r * in_row_bytes and r * out_row_bytes to be multiples of the
  device alignment (256 on RADV). Every Glimmer projection
  geometry clears it at every row: the input widths (6656, 19968)
  and output widths (256 for each KV projection, 4096 for Q, 6656,
  19968) are all multiples of 64 elements, so every f32 row stride
  is a multiple of 1024 bytes and every window offset aligns. A
  hypothetical geometry whose row stride was not a multiple of
  the alignment would refuse at its first misaligned window and
  fall back whole, per projection, by name; no Glimmer projection
  geometry hits that case.
- Scope boundary: `prepare_gated_proj` and `prepare_swiglu_proj`
  are separate routing functions and do NOT route through
  `prepare_proj`; the gated output projection and the SwiGLU pair
  are not chunked by this arm. If the arm wins the head-to-head,
  extending the same rung to those two functions is the follow-up.

## Quantize-once: nothing to reuse, nothing duplicated

The chunked form prepares zero quantize dispatches, so the C3
quantize-once path is neither reused nor violated: there is no
place in this arm where chunking could requantize. The GEMV forms
never consult the HShare and never read the q8 buffers (K1/K2/K3
prepare takes no quantize input); each chunk reads its activation
rows directly from the same resident input buffer the whole-batch
dispatch reads, through a window binding. The quantized forms'
sharing (MMQ riding the layer share, K18 preparing its own) is
untouched, and `ProjCall::dispatches()` counts a chunked call as
exactly its chunk dispatches, no quantize term.

## Dispatch counts per row count, before and after

Per plain projection in the routed band. Before: one GEMV dispatch
at the batch's own row count (or 2 dispatches on the K18 rung when
that env is on: K12 quantize + K18). After, with the chunked env on
and K18 off: one GEMV dispatch per power-of-two chunk.

| rows | before (GEMV) | after (chunked) | decomposition |
|------|---------------|-----------------|---------------|
| 2    | 1             | 1               | [2] |
| 3    | 1             | 2               | [2, 1] |
| 4    | 1             | 1               | [4] |
| 5    | 1             | 2               | [4, 1] |
| 6    | 1             | 2               | [4, 2] |
| 7    | 1             | 3               | [4, 2, 1] |
| 8    | 1             | 1               | [8] |
| 15   | 1             | 4               | [8, 4, 2, 1] |

Routing priority when both small-batch envs are set: K18 first,
then chunked, then whole-batch GEMV, so the head-to-head arms differ
by exactly one env flag each.

## Instrumentation: the brief's claim verified, nothing added

Claim: the diag timestamps system already times each GEMV dispatch
individually, so this arm needs no new instrumentation. VERIFIED in
code: every K1/K2/K3 prepare (including the new `prepare_rows`,
which flows through the same `prepare_inner`) stamps itself through
`ctx.diag_stamp(DispatchMeta { kernel: "k1_q4k_gemv" /
"k2_q6k_gemv" / "k3_q5k_gemv", rows, .. })`, and each windowed call
is its own prepared call with its own stamp, so a chunked batch
appears in the WGPU_COMPUTE_DIAG=timing report as one timed entry
per chunk dispatch. One addition, cosmetic only: the stamp's shape
string for a windowed call carries a ` win@<first_row>` suffix, so
chunks are distinguishable from whole-batch dispatches and from
each other in the report. No timing code was added or changed.

## Correctness gates (VM, 2026-11-05)

This VM enumerates zero Vulkan adapters, so every GPU test in this
crate (the resident session tests, the K18 gates, and the new file
below alike) prints its skip line and passes vacuously here, by the
harness's standing design; the executing proof is the server
protocol's step 0. What the VM gates do prove: full compilation of
lib and tests under clippy -D warnings, the decomposition and
config-resolution unit tests executing, and the whole suite green
with the env OFF (the shipped ladder, byte-identical dispatch
expectations) and the named session suites green with the env ON.

- `cargo test -p wgpu-compute`: PASS. 80 unit tests (including new
  `session::tests::pow2_chunks_decompose_the_verify_band`,
  `session::tests::pow2_chunks_cover_any_batch_contiguously`, and
  `compute::tests::chunked_gemv_max_rows_resolution`) plus all
  integration suites, 0 failed.
- New `crates/wgpu-compute/tests/chunked_gemv.rs`: 4 tests. Per
  family (Q4_K, Q6_K, Q5_K), for batches [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 15],
  the chunked product (windowed prepares at the pow2 decomposition
  into one output buffer) must equal the whole-batch GEMV product
  BIT-EXACTLY (each output element's reduction is independent of
  its batchmates, so anything less than bit equality convicts the
  windowed binding). Plus the refusal gate: empty window, window
  past either buffer, and the alignment refusal asserted
  conditionally from the device's own reported alignment (the
  fixture's 400-byte output rows make row 1 misaligned exactly
  when the device alignment does not divide 400). On this VM:
  skip-pass, as designed; they execute in the server protocol.
- Env OFF (default): the full suite above is the OFF run; routing
  cannot engage (band requires batch <= 1 resolved threshold), so
  dispatch expectations are the shipped ones by construction.
- Env ON: `WGPU_COMPUTE_CHUNKED_GEMV_MAX_ROWS=15 cargo test -p
  wgpu-compute --test resident_session --test resident_block`:
  PASS (resident_session 4/4, resident_block 2/2; skip-pass on this
  VM, executing in the server protocol's step 0).
- `cargo test -p itak-spec`: PASS, 47/47.
- `cargo fmt --check`: clean. `cargo clippy -p wgpu-compute
  --all-targets -- -D warnings`: clean. `cargo check --workspace`:
  clean.

## Head-to-head verdict protocol vs MMV (server, cleared card)

Same discipline as every proof in this repo: one staging tree
synced to the exact commit under test, hash verified, the phase
lock held, one heavy job at a time.

0. Correctness first, per arm, before any timing: identity check
   (raw completion first 8 ids = [13796, 26, 1573, 373, 290, 2167,
   26899, 1212]) and the golden subset agreement on the real GGUF,
   plus this crate's resident session and chunked_gemv tests
   executed on the card with the arm's env on. An arm that fails
   identity does not get timed.
1. Arms, one env flag differing per run, everything else identical
   (same binary except the flag, same prompts, same seed):
   - Control A (shipped): no env. Plain GEMV in the band.
   - Control B (K18): WGPU_COMPUTE_SMALL_BATCH_MAX_ROWS=15.
   - Arm MMV: WGPU_COMPUTE_MMV_MAX_ROWS=15 (lane/mmv-prototype).
   - Arm CHUNKED: WGPU_COMPUTE_CHUNKED_GEMV_MAX_ROWS=15.
2. Measurements per arm: speculative verdict at depths 1 and 6
   (the T-9.6 shape), plain single-token decode re-check, and one
   depth-1 run under WGPU_COMPUTE_DIAG=timing for the per-kernel
   table (the chunked arm's per-chunk GEMV entries vs MMV's kernel
   entries vs K18's quantize+product pairs).
3. Verdict rules, fixed before the runs: the arm that posts the
   best depth-1 and depth-6 verdicts with identity intact wins the
   band. If CHUNKED ties or beats MMV, dispatch shape was the
   defect and the cheap arm ships (default decision then: raise
   DEFAULT_CHUNKED_GEMV_MAX_ROWS to 15 in a follow-up commit). If
   MMV wins clearly, kernel shape was the defect and MMV ships.
   If neither beats Control A, both arms close and the chase moves
   to the next research item (SQTT of the GEMV kernel in the band).

## On-card leg, 2026-11-06: correctness PASS, speed not a win

Step 0 of this note's protocol (the executing on-card
run of the chunked correctness checks) was discharged
through the sweep harness verdict run: from main
`c439e3af45e30275601129568e3e9cb3a89590cb` on the
cleared RX 7900 XTX, the chunked arm
(`WGPU_COMPUTE_CHUNKED_GEMV_MAX_ROWS=16`) ran all 99
cells of the harness matrix and the per-cell
correctness guard against whole-batch GEMV agreed on
every cell (0 disagreeing cells), across all three
quant families, all three shapes, and rows 1-16. The
chunked timing signature is visible in the table
(batch 4 cheaper than batch 3 on the attention shape:
one chunk vs two), proving the decomposition engaged.
Full table: `bench/results/mmv-sweep-20261106-212335/
chunked.csv`, recorded in
`bench/mmv-bench-harness-2026-11-05.md`.

On speed the arm wins 11 of 99 cells against the
other three arms and generally tracks or trails plain
GEMV elsewhere: chunking pays a full weight stream
per chunk, so it only helps where a multi-chunk batch
would otherwise stream per row. It does not beat the
MMV arm in the band and does not change any default
(the flag stays at its shipped off default). The
named follow-up (routing `prepare_gated_proj` and
`prepare_swiglu_proj` through the chunked path) is
not earned by these numbers and stays unbuilt.

  dispatches all day and surface nothing. The wave7
  acceptance proved the machinery works where a collector
  drains it; the follow-up this note files is a drain cadence
  (or an end-of-run drain) in the resident sessions
  themselves. Whether the recorder was created inside these
  example processes cannot be confirmed from their output,
  which is part of the same gap: the run says nothing about
  its instrumentation either way.

# Coopmat prefill build: the device bridge and the Q4_K coopmat kernel (2026-11-06)

Lane: lane/coopmat-build, based on main 09b8d4a.
Specification: bench/coopmat-feasibility-2026-11-06.md
(the verdict: wgpu exposes no cooperative matrix support;
the one honest path is the bridge, create the VkDevice
with ash and VK_KHR_cooperative_matrix enabled, hand it
to wgpu via device_from_raw / create_device_from_hal,
feed hand-compiled SPIR-V through the passthrough path).
This note follows that note's server protocol in order
and stops at the first failed gate.

## Step 0: probe (server, 2026-11-06)

Method: vulkaninfo for the extension list, the feature
struct, and the supported stages; a minimal ash probe
(/tmp/coopmat-probe on the server, ash 0.38.0+1.3.281,
the locked version) for the cooperative matrix property
rows, which this vulkaninfo version does not print.

Device: AMD Radeon RX 7900 XTX (RADV NAVI31), Vulkan
API 1.4.335, subgroupSize 64.

- VK_KHR_cooperative_matrix: EXPOSED, extension
  revision 2.
- VkPhysicalDeviceCooperativeMatrixFeaturesKHR:
  cooperativeMatrix = true,
  cooperativeMatrixRobustBufferAccess = true.
- cooperativeMatrixSupportedStages: SHADER_STAGE_
  COMPUTE_BIT (count 1).
- Property rows: 14, all M=N=K=16, all scope SUBGROUP.
  Twelve are int8 forms (UINT8/SINT8 A and B to
  UINT32/SINT32 results, three of them with saturating
  accumulation). The two f16 forms:
  - A FLOAT16, B FLOAT16, C FLOAT16, result FLOAT16
  - A FLOAT16, B FLOAT16, C FLOAT32, result FLOAT32
- The row this build needs (f16 16x16x16, f32
  accumulate, compute) is the second f16 row. Present.

Toolchain: /usr/bin/glslangValidator, /usr/bin/glslc,
/usr/bin/spirv-dis, /usr/bin/spirv-val are all present
as system tools on the server (not only inside the
llama.cpp build tree).

### Spec-update addendum (llama parity lane, same day)

bench/llama-parity-specs-2026-11-06.md pins the exact
shader llama runs for prefill on this card family:
mul_mmq_cm1.comp, the INTEGER coopmat MMQ, not the
generic f16 mul_mm coopmat. Enablement in ggml is
VK_KHR_cooperative_matrix present + the device feature
cooperativeMatrix on (ggml-vulkan.cpp:4087-4093, 4556);
a subgroup-scope s8 x s8 to s32 16x16x16 shape sets
coopmat_int_support (:4740-4748); on RDNA3/4 the Q4_K,
Q5_K, and Q6_K by Q8_1 products run mul_mmq_cm1.comp
(:1877, :2481-2494) with BM 128, BN 128, BK 32 and
TM/TN/TK = 16 (mul_mmq_cm1.comp:89-100).

Consequence for this lane: the required property row
is the s8 x s8 to s32 16x16x16 subgroup row, not the
f16 row. The probe above recorded twelve int8 rows;
among them the required one is present in both
saturating variants:

- A SINT8, B SINT8, C SINT32, result SINT32,
  saturating accumulation 0, scope SUBGROUP
- A SINT8, B SINT8, C SINT32, result SINT32,
  saturating accumulation 1, scope SUBGROUP

The shader does not request saturating accumulation;
either variant satisfies the gate. The bridge's
runtime probe (step 1) checks for this row.

**Step 0 verdict: PASS.** Extension, required matrix
row (the integer row, per the addendum), and compiler
all present. Proceeding to step 1.

## Step 1: the device bridge

Built in crates/wgpu-compute/src/coopmat_bridge.rs,
wired into GpuContext::open in device.rs. Design, as
implemented:

- Two switches, deliberately separate. The bridge
  switch is WGPU_COMPUTE_COOPMAT_BRIDGE (exact value
  1, fail closed, the K22 resolver idiom); the routing
  switch WGPU_COMPUTE_COOPMAT arrives with the kernel
  in step 2. The bridge smoke in step 3 needs a bridged
  device with routing still off, which is why they are
  not one switch.
- Mechanism: the feasibility note costed creating the
  VkDevice by hand with ash and wrapping it through
  device_from_raw. The implementation uses wgpu-hal's
  own end-to-end form of the same mechanism: the hal
  adapter's `open_with_callback` runs hal's own device
  creation (its extension computation, feature
  selection, and queue setup are the stock ones), and
  the CreateDeviceCallback adds
  VK_KHR_cooperative_matrix to the extension list and
  chains VkPhysicalDeviceCooperativeMatrixFeaturesKHR
  with cooperativeMatrix = true into the create info;
  `open_with_callback` ends in device_from_raw
  internally, and Adapter::create_device_from_hal
  wraps the result. The bridged device differs from
  the stock device by exactly the coopmat extension
  and feature; nothing else about device creation is
  reimplemented. The callback runs synchronously
  inside the open call, so the chained feature struct
  (a local) outlives every use of the chain.
- Runtime probes, all before any device is created:
  the extension is enumerated on the chosen physical
  device; the cooperativeMatrix feature bit is read
  through VkPhysicalDeviceFeatures2; the subgroup size
  through VkPhysicalDeviceProperties2; the property
  rows through the KHR query, requiring the s8 x s8 to
  s32 16x16x16 subgroup row above. Any refusal returns
  by name; GpuContext::open logs it on the diag
  channel ("coopmat bridge refused: ...; the stock
  device serves") and opens the stock device, so a
  machine without coopmat serves exactly as before,
  with the refusal on record. GpuContext.coopmat is
  Some only on a bridged device; the kernel gates its
  existence on that, so routing against a stock device
  refuses by name in step 2, never silently.
- When the bridge succeeds, the device also requests
  EXPERIMENTAL_PASSTHROUGH_SHADERS (masked by the
  adapter's granted features) over the stock feature
  set; the passthrough module path is how the coopmat
  SPIR-V enters. With the switch unset, the
  request_device call is the shipped one, unchanged.
- Unsafe: the crate moves from forbid(unsafe_code) to
  deny(unsafe_code) (the GGUF mmap precedent), and all
  unsafe is confined to open_bridged under
  #[allow(unsafe_code)], with the safety contract for
  each call written in that function's docs. New
  direct dependencies ash = "0.38" and wgpu-hal =
  "27": both already in the workspace lockfile as
  transitive dependencies of wgpu 27, so no new
  packages enter the tree.

First compile caught one defect, fixed in the same
unit: VkPhysicalDeviceSubgroupProperties chains into
the properties pNext family, not the features one
(the compiler rejected it in the features2 chain);
the subgroup size is now read through a separate
get_physical_device_properties2 call.

VM gates for this unit (run with the step-2 unit,
which shares the build): recorded under step 2.

Committed as lane unit 25a51c1.

## Step 2: the coopmat shader and kernel

The shader: crates/wgpu-compute/src/kernels/coopmat/
k23_q4k_coopmat.comp, a standalone GLSL port of
llama's mul_mmq_cm1 design specialized to Q4_K x
Q8_1, single batch per call, this backend's buffer
contract (the same five bindings K13 prepares:
weights, K12 qs, K12 ds, output, params).

Transcribed from llama (mul_mmq_cm1.comp and the
Q4_K parts of mul_mmq_cm1_funcs.glsl, read in full
before writing):

- Staging split: weight codes de-interleaved into
  shared rows of QPITCH = BK_STEP * (BK / 4) + 4 = 36
  u32 words (the +4 bank skew), per-sub-block
  (d * scale, -(dmin * min)) pairs in a separate vec2
  array (buf_a_dm's role); activation Q8_1 words in
  the mirrored tile, (d, d * sum) pairs in two float
  arrays (buf_b_d / buf_b_s's role). Nibbles stage
  raw (0..15 as int8 bytes); the min correction
  absorbs the unsigned offset, as llama's Q4_K
  block_a_to_shmem does. This repo's K12 writes the
  activation sum pre-scaled by d, the same convention
  ggml's MMQ quantizer uses, so the pairs move
  unchanged (K13's epilogue is the in-repo proof of
  the convention).
- The accumulate identity, per 32-element sub-block:
  out += dot_i32 * (d_b * sc) * d_a
       + (-(dmin_b * mn)) * (d_a * sum_q),
  llama's cm1_accumulate for Q4_K, and K13's
  vec_dot_q4_K_q8_1 fold with the signs folded into
  the staged pair.
- Tiles BK 32, BK_STEP 4 (a staged chunk is 128 K
  elements), TM = TN = TK = 16.

Adapted, with the reasons stated:

- Workgroup tile 128 output rows x 64 batch rows
  (llama runs 128 x 128): this backend's MMQ band
  caps the batch at 64 (K13's MMQ_MAX_BATCH
  contract), so the batch side halves. Two subgroups
  across each side; each subgroup owns 64 x 32
  outputs (llama's WM 64 / WN 32 warp tile).
- The accumulator epilogue is a deliberate
  simplification. llama extracts the int32
  accumulator's elements per thread, which needs the
  wave-size-dependent element mapping (cm_elem_row)
  and, at wave 64, the magic-bias path. This shader
  coopMatStores each 16x16 int32 tile into a
  per-subgroup shared tile and folds it with scalar
  reads, which is layout-exact under the cooperative
  matrix memory rules and carries no element-mapping
  assumptions. The extraction form is the named
  follow-up if the step-3 profile convicts the fold.
- Dequant header math (f16 d/dmin via
  unpackHalf2x16, get_scale_min_k4) is transcribed
  from this repo's proven K13 WGSL, not from llama's
  GLSL.

Compile (on the server, system glslangValidator,
target vulkan1.3): clean after one catch, recorded
here because it is the kind of thing the next port
will hit: gl_ScopeSubgroup in the coopmat types
requires GL_KHR_memory_scope_semantics, which
llama's header enables and the first draft here
omitted. spirv-val passes. The artifact
(k23_q4k_coopmat.spv, 19,836 bytes) is checked in
with its source, its full disassembly
(k23_q4k_coopmat.spv.dis.txt), and rebuild.sh, which
recompiles, validates, disassembles, and greps for
the ops. Disassembly inspection: OpCapability
CooperativeMatrixKHR present; OpTypeCooperativeMatrixKHR
declared for int32 16x16 accumulator and int8 16x16
A and B, all subgroup scope; OpCooperativeMatrixLoadKHR,
OpCooperativeMatrixStoreKHR, and
OpCooperativeMatrixMulAddKHR all present.

The Rust side: kernels/k23_q4k_coopmat.rs (K23).
Pipeline construction happens only on a bridged
device (backend construction reads GpuContext.coopmat;
on a stock device the pipeline is never attempted,
since a passthrough module against a device without
the extension would be a spec violation). The
constructor additionally refuses by name on a
subgroup size other than 64 (the shader's compiled
geometry) or workgroup storage under the 37,888
bytes the shader stages. The bind group layout is
declared explicitly in Rust rather than reflected,
because the passthrough module's bindings are the
GLSL contract. The passthrough call itself is the
crate's second unsafe site and lives in
coopmat_bridge.rs, under a written contract (the
words are a checked-in, spirv-val-validated artifact,
fed only to bridge-opened devices).

Routing: session.rs's Q4_K ladder gains a first
rung. When WGPU_COMPUTE_COOPMAT=1 (fail-closed
resolver in compute.rs, the K22 idiom, config echoed
at backend construction), the coopmat prepare is
tried first; a prepare refusal, or the switch on
with no pipeline (stock device), logs by name and
the shipped ladder serves. Default off; K13 remains
the default and the fallback. Diag stamp
k23_q4k_coopmat, registered through the same
DispatchMeta path as every kernel.

On-card numeric gates: tests/k23_coopmat.rs, the
K22 test's mirror: K23 against the host reference
running the same quantized math and against K13, at
input width 6656 with batches 64 and 62 (the
prefill chunk and its tail), K13 parity on the full
6656 x 6656 square at batch 64, and the batch-band
refusals by name. The tests skip with the reason
printed on stock devices and on machines without a
suitable adapter, by design.

VM gates (this machine has no GPU; Naga validation
of the WGSL fleet is the standing stand-in, and it
structurally cannot cover K23, the feasibility
note's disclosed gate hole): cargo test -p
wgpu-compute --lib, 106 passed / 0 failed, including
the new unit tests (the bridge resolver, the coopmat
routing resolver, K23's shape contract and grid
math, and a SPIR-V instruction-stream walk requiring
the four coopmat opcodes in the checked-in artifact);
clippy --all-targets clean under the workspace's
deny-warnings lints; cargo fmt --check clean after
one formatting pass over the bridge callback.

Committed as lane unit 6cc13cf.

tests/k23_coopmat.rs on the bridged device:

- vs the host reference running the same quantized
  math, width 6656, out 512: batch 64 max abs diff
  3.125e-2 at set scale 4.173e4 (rel 7.5e-7); batch

### Leg 3: the 1,022-token prefill A/B. K23 LOSES.

Diag-timing runs through prefill_profile, same
prompt, same binary, only the env differs:

| arm | Q4_K kernel line | wall (timing mode) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| control (env unset) | k13_q4k_mmq: 2,912 dispatches, 4,250.1 ms, 45.9 GB/s | 7,164 ms |
| coopmat (bridge + routing) | k23_q4k_coopmat: 2,912 dispatches, 16,951.3 ms, 11.5 GB/s | 19,851 ms |

Diag-off walls of record: control 6,453 ms, coopmat
19,518 ms. The Q6_K line is unchanged across arms
(1,360.8 vs 1,382.8 ms), so the delta is the Q4_K
product alone: the coopmat kernel is 4.0x slower than
K13 at the kernel line and 3.0x slower at the wall.
Dispatch totals are identical (10,448 in every arm
and mode): routing swaps the kernel, never the plan.

Why, as labeled hypotheses (no ACO autopsy was run
on this module; the verdict does not need one): the
port's two disclosed simplifications are the prime
suspects. The LDS fold runs per sub-block: eight
tile stores, sixteen subgroup barriers, and a fold
in which half the subgroup idles per tile, all
serializing the matrix units' output. And the port
interleaves load, muladd, store, and fold per tile,
where llama preloads a sub-block's fragments into
register arrays before the muladds. The grid is also
half K13's at the wide shapes (52 workgroups at out
6656 against the m64 shape's 104, both LDS-capped at
one workgroup per CU). The named follow-ups, in
order: the element-extraction epilogue in llama's
cm_elem_row form; fragment preload arrays; an ACO
statistics pass (VGPR, spills, scratch) through
pipeline executable properties.

With every coopmat variable unset, this tree
reproduces the shipped marks: prefill wall 6,349 ms
(glimmer_generate) and 6,453 ms (prefill_profile)
against the recorded 6,330; the K13 kernel line
4,250.1 ms / 45.9 GB/s against the recorded
4,199.9 ms / 46.4 GB/s; dispatch totals 10,448 in
both diag modes; generated ids [7235, 19596, 30054,
28], exact. The bridge's off path is byte-identical
in behavior, as designed.

### Session identity under coopmat routing. EXACT.

glimmer_generate --gpu with the bridge and routing
on, the full 1,022-token prompt: prefill 19,401 ms
through K23 for every Q4_K projection, generated ids
[7235, 19596, 30054, 28], the golden sequence. The
kernel is end-to-end correct through the real model,
not only against synthetic fixtures. (One harness
error recorded for honesty: the first
glimmer_generate invocation omitted --gpu and ran
the CPU backend at 100% CPU with the card idle; it
was killed and rerun with the flag. No measurement
was taken from it.)

### Tenants restored.

docker start on both Cortex containers and
systemctl --user start cortex-embed.service: both
containers Up (healthy), the service active, VRAM

## Lane verdict

The bridge works and is the durable result: it is
the only legal door to VK_KHR_cooperative_matrix on
this wgpu stack, it opens with named fail-closed
probes, its off path is provably the shipped path,
and the full resident suite passes on a bridged
device. The K23 kernel is CORRECT, against the host
reference, against K13, and through the real model's
greedy identity. It is also 4x SLOWER than K13 at the
product it exists to accelerate.

Per the decision rule written before the run
(material A/B win required for a default flip), the
recommendation is: WGPU_COMPUTE_COOPMAT stays off by
default, K13 remains the shipped Q4_K MMQ, and the
coopmat path stays in the tree behind its two
switches as the measured starting point for the
follow-up iteration (extraction epilogue and
fragment preload), which now has a correct reference
implementation to optimize against.
