===== FILE: bench/splitk-mmq-2026-11-07.md =====
# Split-K for the MMQ prompt path (K13 Q4_K, K14 Q6_K) - design, factor rule, drift analysis, and the card verdict protocol

Lane `lane/splitk-mmq`, built 2026-11-07 from main
`0ecdc8ff5efc3da0d00b5806c8f2796b65096132`. State: code
complete and VM-gated (counts below); the card verdict
protocol is written and NOT yet run (the parent
serializes card time in a consolidated session). The
routing config defaults OFF; nothing in the shipped
ladder changes with the env unset.

## The problem, from the measurements

The prefill profile (`bench/prefill-profile-2026-11-05.md`,
carried in `bench/baseline-session-2026-11-06.md`) put
83.2% of the 1,022-token prefill's GPU time in the MMQ
pair, K13 (Q4_K) and K14 (Q6_K) streaming at ~43.5 GB/s
combined against a card that streams a GEMV at ~650
GB/s in the same runs. The worst single shape is the
256-wide Q6_K KV projection: 416 dispatches at 3.2 GB/s,
about 186 ms of the prefill.

The shape math explains it. An MMQ workgroup owns a
whole output tile (64 rows at the shipped m64 shape)
and walks the entire reduction serially: for a 256-row
output the grid is 4 workgroups, each walking all 26
super-block columns of the 6656-wide input. Four
workgroups on a 96-CU card is about 4% occupancy of the
machine for that dispatch, and no register or staging
organization fixes a grid that small. llama.cpp's
`mul_mm` has a split path for exactly this reason; this
lane takes the design (partition the reduction, write
partials, reduce) and re-derives it in this tree's WGSL
and routing idiom, not the GLSL code.

## Design

**Split product.** The split shader is generated from
the same generator as the plain product
(`mmq_shader_split(shape, split)` in each kernel
module), so staging, the DP4A inner product, and the
per-sub-block fold are byte-for-byte the plain kernel's
code. Three things change:

- The `Params` uniform gains `splits: u32`. The factor
  is a runtime parameter, not a generated literal, so
  one compiled pipeline per family serves every factor.
- The super-block loop walks the workgroup's slice of
  the range: slice `s` (the grid's `wid.y`) covers
  `[s * per_split, min((s+1) * per_split, blocks))`
  with `per_split = ceil(blocks / splits)`. Slices
  partition the columns disjointly and completely; a
  slice past the end (factor greater than the block
  count) walks an empty range and stores its zero
  accumulators, so any factor in range is correct for
  any width.
- The stores index a partials buffer laid out
  `[splits][batch][out_rows]` instead of the output.

**Reduction.** `kernels/splitk_reduce.rs`: one thread
per output element sums the slices in ascending order
(`acc = p[0][i]; acc += p[1][i]; ...`), workgroup 256,
grid `ceil(total / 256)`. Pure bandwidth: at the KV
shape with factor 8 and a 64-row chunk it reads
8 x 64 x 256 x 4 B = 512 KB and writes 64 KB. The order
is fixed by construction (no atomics, no tree), so a
split run is deterministic run to run.

**Ownership.** The partials scratch is allocated by the
split prepare (`splits * batch * out_rows` f32) and
lives in the returned call's bind groups, mirroring how
the existing calls own their params buffers. The split
call type (`K13SplitCall` / `K14SplitCall`) encodes
product then reduction into the caller's open pass;
dispatches within one pass are ordered, the same
composition the K12 quantize + product chain relies on.
Both split pipelines and the reducer compile inside
`K13Pipeline::with_shape` / `K14Pipeline::with_shape`
regardless of the routing config, so a shader defect in
either form fails at backend construction, not at first
routed use.

**Routing seam.** The split is a property of the
standard product, not a new rung: inside
`mmq_product_q4k` / `mmq_product_q6k`, after the
coopmat / wide / K22 / K23 rungs have had their say,
the standard rung asks the backend for the projection's
factor and prepares the split form when it is 2 or
more, falling back to the unsplit prepare with the
refusal logged by name. It deliberately does NOT stack
on the opt-in prototypes (coopmat, K22, K23, wide):
those are unproven forms, and stacking two unproven
dispatch shapes would make any card result
unattributable. The session gains two `ProjCall`
variants (`MmqSplitQ4K`, `MmqSplitQ6K`) whose dispatch
accounting is product + reduction (+ quantize when
carried), and whose kernel names are the split stamps.

**Config.** `WGPU_COMPUTE_MMQ_SPLITK`, resolved once at
backend construction in the codebase's fail-closed
pattern:

- unset or `off` -> off (the default);
- `1`..=`8` -> a fixed factor;
- `auto` -> the per-projection rule below;
- anything else -> off, with the unrecognized value
  named in the construction log
  (`log_mmq_splitk_fallback`, the flash/K21F pattern).

The resolved mode is recorded as the `mmq_splitk` pair
(`off` / `fixed:N` / `auto`) in the diag manifest's
`resolved_config`, in both the resident and dflash
sessions, beside `k22_mmq` and `k21f_head`. Diag stamps
distinguish split dispatches: `k13_q4k_mmq_split` and
`k14_q6k_mmq_split` for the products (their shape field
carries `splits=N`), `splitk_reduce` for the reduction.

## The factor rule and its rationale

`mmq_splitk_factor(mode, tiles, blocks_per_row)` in
`compute.rs`, where `tiles` is the unsplit grid size
(output rows / tile) and `blocks_per_row` the
super-block columns:

- Off -> 1.
- Fixed(n) -> `n` clamped to `[1, min(8, blocks)]`:
  past the block count the extra slices are empty, so
  the cap is efficiency, not correctness.
- Auto -> `ceil(64 / tiles)` clamped to
  `[1, min(8, blocks)]`: target roughly 64 workgroups,
  about two-thirds of the card's CUs, leaving the
  scheduler room to overlap the tail.

Against the Glimmer shapes (tile 64, prefill chunks):

| projection | out | in | tiles | blocks | auto factor | split grid |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| K/V proj (Q6_K) | 256 | 6656 | 4 | 26 | 8 | 32 |
| Q proj (Q4_K) | 6656 | 6656 | 104 | 26 | 1 | 104 |
| O proj (Q4_K) | 6656 | 6656 | 104 | 26 | 1 | 104 |
| FFN gate/up (Q4_K) | 19968 | 6656 | 312 | 26 | 1 | 312 |
| FFN down (Q4_K) | 6656 | 19968 | 104 | 78 | 1 | 104 |
| any out <= 2048 | <=2048 | any | <=32 | any | >=2 | >=64 |

Under auto, exactly the starved shapes split and
everything already filling the card is untouched. At
the KV shape with factor 8 the slices walk
4/4/4/4/4/4/2/0 blocks (per_split = ceil(26/8) = 4):
the last slice is empty and the seventh walks 2, a
known imbalance the card A/B should weigh against
factor 4 (7/7/6/6, grid 16) and factor 2 (13/13,
grid 8). The fixed mode exists so the verdict can
sweep the factor directly instead of trusting the
rule.

**Costs, stated.** Total staged bytes are unchanged:
slices partition the columns, so every super-block
column is staged exactly once across the grid, by
exactly one slice (weights and activations alike).
The new traffic is the partials round trip:
`splits x batch x out_rows` f32 written and re-read,
plus one reduction dispatch per projection. At the KV
shape, factor 8, batch 64: about 1 MB of extra traffic
against 13.7 MB of weight bytes the dispatch streams -
worth paying only if the occupancy win is real, which
is the card's question, not this note's claim.

## Drift analysis

The split product is NOT bit-identical to the unsplit
product, and this lane does not claim it is:

- The integer dots are exact and identical: each
  slice's DP4A sums cover the same elements with the
  same operands as the unsplit kernel's.
- Within a slice, the f32 fold sequence (per
  sub-block, ascending super-block order) is the
  unsplit kernel's sequence restricted to that slice's
  columns: same terms, same order, same expressions.
- What changes is only the grouping of the f32
  accumulation: the unsplit kernel folds all 26
  super-blocks into one chain; the split form folds
  each slice into its own chain starting from 0.0 and
  adds the slice sums in ascending slice order. f32
  addition is not associative, so the results differ
  by reassociation noise - the same drift class the
  existing MMQ gate already bounds against the host
  reference running the same quantized math
  (`check_close`: `2e-3 + 5e-5 x set scale`).
- Empty slices contribute exact zeros: a stored 0.0
  partial added to a finite sum changes nothing (the
  only edge is the sign of a zero result when every
  partial is zero, which is +0.0 in both forms: both
  accumulation chains start at +0.0).

Bit-identity would require reproducing the unsplit
chain's exact left-to-right order across slices, which
serializes the accumulation and defeats the split. The
identity question for the card session is therefore
the standing one for reassociation-class changes: does
the token stream stay identical on the golden prompts
(the same evidence standard the shipped defaults
already carry - outputs token-identical with
probability deltas inside the f32 accumulation-noise
band).

The gate in `tests/splitk_mmq.rs` pins the split
product against the host quantized-math reference AND
against the unsplit GPU product, both at the
reassociation bound, at: the KV shape (6656 in, 256
out) at factors 2, 4 (Q6_K), and 8; a ragged width
(1280 in = 5 blocks, factor 4: ranges 2/2/1/empty);
and a factor past the block count (768 in = 3 blocks,
factor 8: five empty slices). On this VM the tests
skip GPU execution (no adapter) by the suite's
standing pattern; their GPU legs are owed on the card
(see below).

## Autopsy readiness (what the VM could prove)

Naga validation runs green here for every generated
variant (plain and split, m32 and m64, both families,
plus the reducer): the module unit tests
`plain_and_split_shaders_validate_under_naga` parse and
validate each generated shader with
`ValidationFlags::all()`. That proves the WGSL is
well-formed and well-typed; it cannot prove driver
acceptance or register behavior.

The register expectation, from the generated code: the
split shader is the plain shader's body plus three
index scalars (`per_split`, `blk_first`, `blk_last`)
and a multiply in the store index. The accumulator
shape is unchanged (16 f32 accumulators, the unrolled
16-wide i32 dot set per sub-block), and the workgroup
storage is unchanged (the same staging arrays:
41,216 B at m64 for Q4_K, 45,312 B for Q6_K). So the
split forms should land at the plain kernels' VGPR/LDS
picture (the plain Q4_K MMQ compiles at the VGPR 256
cap per the K22/K23 autopsies) with no new spill
pressure - but a compiler is free to surprise, and
spills are exactly what this VM cannot see. The
reduction kernel is one accumulator and streaming
reads; nothing about it can spill meaningfully.

One defect this lane caught in itself, recorded
because the gate pattern matters: the first Naga run
failed at end-of-file on BOTH plain and split shaders -
the split generator's loop header was a `format!`
VALUE carrying a doubled brace (`{{`), which survives
substitution literally and unbalances the shader. The
plain shader's identical header (moved into the same
value during the parameterization) broke with it. The
Naga tests now also assert no `{{` / `}}` appears in
any generated shader, so the escape-leak class is
pinned by name, not rediscovered by parse error.

## Judgment calls in this lane

- Split applies at the standard rung only, never
  stacked on the coopmat/wide/K22/K23 prototypes:
  attribution of any card result stays clean.
- Contiguous ceil-division slice ranges (llama's
  design shape) over a balanced interleave: within a
  slice the fold order matches the unsplit kernel's,
  keeping the drift argument one sentence long; the
  tail imbalance at 26 blocks / factor 8 is accepted
  and named above for the A/B to weigh.
- Partials scratch is per-prepare (the K13 params
  buffer precedent), not a plan-owned arena: plans
  stay free of a new lifetime, at the cost of one
  allocation per split projection per plan build.
- The auto rule's 64-workgroup target is a heuristic
  from the shape table, not a measured optimum; the
  fixed mode is the verdict's sweep instrument.
- Q5_K has no MMQ product in this tree's prompt path,
  so there is no Q5_K split form; inventing one was
  out of scope by the tasking.

===== FILE: bench/structured-output-2026-10-28.md =====
# Structured Output: JSON mode vs JSON Schema vs few-shot, docs + live experiment (2026-10-28)

Question (David): which technique gets better results per model, plain JSON mode, formal
JSON Schema constraining, or few-shot/template prompting in the prompt? His prior: the Qwen
models do better with template structure. Verdict up front: **he is right, and the mechanism
is documented by the vendors themselves, but the biggest measured effect is not JSON shape
at all. It is reasoning budget starvation, and the few-shot example is what fixes it.**

## Part 1: What the documentation says (researched 2026-10-28, primary sources)

- **Qwen (3.8 / 3.6 / 2.5 family):** JSON Object mode is officially documented and
  contractually requires the word "json" somewhere in the prompt or the hosted API errors
  out. Schema mode is officially documented for "selected models only" on the hosted API;
  locally the engine enforces any schema regardless. Community guidance for Qwen 3.8 27B
  specifically recommends an output contract in the prompt + json_object + few-shot
  examples. (docs.qwencloud.com structured output guide; Alibaba Model Studio docs.)
- **DeepSeek:** the official JSON Output guide requires (1) response_format json_object,
  (2) the word "json" in the prompt, (3) **an example of the desired JSON format in the
  prompt**, (4) a max_tokens high enough not to truncate. Few-shot is the documented
  operating procedure for this family, not an optional extra. No native strict schema mode.
  (api-docs.deepseek.com/guides/json_mode)
- **Mistral / Devstral:** both JSON mode and schema ("custom") structured outputs are
  officially documented; Mistral states schema mode "is more reliable and is recommended
  whenever possible." Devstral is non-thinking, so grammars constrain safely from token
  zero. (docs.mistral.ai structured output pages)
- **gpt-oss:** everything runs through the Harmony format; reasoning lives in the
  `analysis` channel, the answer in `final`, and a message header can carry
  `<|constrain|>json` to switch exactly that span into JSON-constrained sampling. It is
  the cleanest design in the set for structured output: the engine constrains the answer
  channel while reasoning runs free. (OpenAI gpt-oss cookbook)
- **Glimmer:** provider listings confirm JSON-schema structured outputs, but the model
  speaks channel-scoped turns with a native ATEM tool-call format (not JSON tool calls),
  and a documented failure mode is max_tokens clipping mid-thought into empty content.
  (OpenRouter model page; vLLM recipe requires the muse_glimmer parsers.)
- **Gemma 4:** no vendor JSON-mode doc for the open weights (hosted Gemini docs do not
  transfer). What Google documents is trained-in function calling with dedicated tool
  tokens and a `<|"|>` string delimiter, plus a `<|think|>` control token. Local
  enforcement is engine grammar only. (ai.google.dev Gemma docs)
- **Nemotron Cascade 2:** NVIDIA trained structured output in via a dedicated RL stage
  (tool calling + structured output); ChatML template, tool calls wrapped in `<tool_call>`
  tags rather than bare JSON. No model-specific JSON-mode doc found.
- **North Mini Code:** weakest documented position. OpenRouter's route states the model
  "does not support response_format"; the model card recommends tool descriptions as JSON
  schema but documents no JSON mode. Engine grammar is the only enforcement path.
- **Engine reality (llama.cpp):** llama-server converts response_format json_schema into
  a GBNF grammar that masks logits token by token. json_object without a schema applies
  only the generic JSON grammar. The guarantee is **syntax and shape, never value
  correctness**, and a truncated generation (max_tokens) is still unparseable. The
  schema converter silently skips unsupported JSON Schema features. For thinking models
  the grammar path is the hard part: llama.cpp's lazy grammars (which wait for a trigger
  before constraining) exist on the tool-calling path; a plain response_format request
  fights the think block, and reasoning + content share one completion budget.
  (llama.cpp grammars README; JSONSchemaBench, arXiv:2501.10868, found constrained
  decoding beat unconstrained generation on task quality for every engine tested.)

## Part 2: Live experiment (ubuntu-server, 2026-10-28)

Setup: llama.cpp a7af149 Vulkan, GPU exclusive, temp 0, 512-token budget, each model's own
chat template. Task: extract a lead from a customer message into 6 fields (name, phone,
service, city, urgency enum, callback_ok). 3 cases: A emergency with full data, B low
urgency with full data, C a pool question with **no phone number** (hallucination probe:
correct phone value is null). 4 techniques x 3 cases x 10 models = 120 runs.
Scores: parse = valid JSON extracted; keys = all 6 keys present; fields = correct values
of 18 (3 cases x 6 fields). Raw runs: `/mnt/models/structured-2026-10-28/results/`.

| Model | Plain | JSON mode | JSON Schema | Few-shot |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Muse-Glimmer-30B | 1/3 parse, 6/18 | 1/3, 6/18 | 1/3, 5/18 | **3/3, 17/18** |
| Qwen3.8-27B | 2/3, 11/18 | 2/3, 11/18 | 1/3, 4/18 | 2/3, 11/18 |
| Qwen3.6-27B | 0/3, 0/18 | 0/3, 0/18 | 0/3, 0/18 | 1/3, 6/18 |
| Gemma-4-31B-it | 2/3, 11/18 | 2/3, 11/18 | **3/3, 16/18** | 2/3, 11/18 |
| Qwen2.5-Coder-32B | 3/3, 15/18 | 3/3, 15/18 | **3/3, 17/18** | 3/3, 15/18 |
| Nemotron-Cascade-2 | 2/3, 10/18 | 2/3, 10/18 | 2/3, 9/18 | **3/3, 15/18** |
| North-Mini-Code-1.0 | 3/3, 14/18 | 3/3, 14/18 | 3/3, 15/18 | 2/3, 10/18 |
| Devstral-Small-2 | 3/3, 15/18 | 3/3, 15/18 | 3/3, 15/18 | 3/3, 15/18 |
| DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite | 3/3, 13/18 | 3/3, 13/18 | **3/3, 16/18** | 3/3, 15/18 |
| gpt-oss-20b | 3/3, 15/18 | 3/3, 15/18 | 3/3, 15/18 | 3/3, 15/18 |

## What the runs actually show

1. **The dominant failure is reasoning eating the budget, not bad JSON.** Qwen3.8's schema
   run on case A: 512 output tokens produced, 2,022 characters of reasoning, **empty
   content**. Qwen3.6 did this on 11 of 12 runs across every technique. Glimmer's plain
   run began emitting perfect JSON and still failed because 2,089 characters of reasoning
   came first inside the same budget. Almost every response that produced content at all
   parsed cleanly. Shape is nearly free; finished answers are the scarce resource.
2. **Few-shot is the single biggest lever for channel/thinking models.** Glimmer went
   from 6/18 (plain) to **17/18, the best cell in the experiment**, and its reasoning
   dropped to zero characters: the worked example switched it into direct-answer mode.
   Nemotron gained the same way (10 to 15). This matches the vendor docs: for Qwen and
   DeepSeek families the in-prompt example is part of the documented mechanism.
3. **JSON Schema is the best lever for capable-but-sloppy non-thinking models.** Gemma
   11 to 16, DeepSeek 13 to 16, Qwen2.5-Coder 15 to 17 (best total with Glimmer-few-shot),
   North 14 to 15. The grammar guarantees the shape; these models supply the values.
4. **JSON mode (json_object) changed nothing anywhere.** Identical scores to plain for
   8 of 10 models. In llama.cpp it adds only the generic JSON grammar, and these models
   already emit JSON-shaped text when asked. It is a checkbox, not an improvement.
5. **Devstral and gpt-oss are technique-proof:** 15/18 under all four techniques. Their
   remaining misses are value judgments, not format. For a set-and-forget extraction
   endpoint they are the safe defaults.
6. **Nobody hallucinated.** In all 120 runs, no model invented a phone number for the
   phoneless case; every parsed answer used null. The extraction risk on this task class
   is not fabrication.
7. **The real accuracy leak is undefined judgment fields.** Across all parsed runs the
   misses concentrate in exactly two fields: callback_ok (28 misses on case C, 20 on
   case A) and urgency on the ambiguous case C (23). Name, phone, service, and city were
   near-perfect everywhere. Models split on whether callback_ok means "has a number"
   (ground truth) or "seems willing," and whether a signal-free message is low or normal
   urgency. That is a prompt-specification problem: define the fields in the prompt
   ("callback_ok: true only when a phone number is present") and most of the remaining
   error in this table should collapse. Stated as a prediction, not a measurement.

## Recommendation for AlphaFlux lead extraction

Stack all three, each doing the job the others cannot:

1. **JSON Schema grammar on** (llama-server response_format json_schema): hard guarantee
   on keys, types, and the urgency enum.
2. **Field definitions in the prompt**, one line each, especially for judgment fields.
3. **One worked example** (few-shot): suppresses reasoning starvation on thinking and
   channel models, teaches value conventions.
4. **Budget discipline:** thinking models get reasoning disabled for extraction, or a
   completion budget of 1024+; 512 starves them before the grammar ever applies.

Model pick on this evidence: Qwen2.5-Coder-32B + schema (17/18) or Glimmer + few-shot
(17/18, and it is the house model) for quality; Devstral or gpt-oss (15/18 under any
technique, fastest operations) when the pipeline cannot babysit configuration. Avoid
Qwen3.6 for structured work until its reasoning is controlled; avoid relying on
json_object mode to fix anything.

## Appendix: model swap cycle, stopwatch (same day, David's question)

Full cycle = server start to ready, one question answered, process killed, VRAM verified
back at the 31 MiB baseline:

| Model | Load to ready | Question | Unload to VRAM-free | Full cycle |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen2.5-Coder-32B (19.9 GB, largest) | 4.10 s | 0.87 s | 0.36 s | **5.33 s** |
| gpt-oss-20b (12.1 GB) | 2.77 s | 0.52 s | 0.36 s | **3.65 s** |

Swapping models per task on this box costs single-digit seconds; per-task model routing
is practical.

## Panel open questions OQ-2 and OQ-3: two metadata values at full precision

Read from the real Glimmer file during this same window, at the
critic panel's request. Keys enumerated with llama.cpp's own
`llama-gguf` (build-vulkan2/bin/llama-gguf, read mode, 32 kv
pairs); values read from the GGUF header with a stdlib Python
parser that prints the raw bits (gguf_meta.py, kept in the run's
staging tree). Both tools agree on the key names and order.

- **OQ-2, attention RMS norm epsilon.** Key
  `muse-glimmer.attention.layer_norm_rms_epsilon` (kv[11], GGUF
  type FLOAT32): **9.999999747378752e-06**, raw f32 bits
  `0x3727c5ac`. That is exactly the f32 nearest 1e-5, so the
  rebuild's asserted 1e-5 (crates/muse-glimmer/src/config.rs,
  which reads this key and asserts the parsed value within 1e-9
  of 1e-5) is confirmed against the primary source: the file
  carries 1e-5 at f32 precision, nothing else.
- **OQ-3, logit scale.** Key `muse-glimmer.logit_scale`
  (kv[15], GGUF type FLOAT32): **0.1961161345243454**, raw f32
  bits `0x3e48d2ab`. The code carries 0.19611613
  (crates/muse-glimmer/src/config.rs doc and test constant,
  asserted within 1e-6; actual difference 4.5e-9), which is this
  f32 rounded to 8 decimal places, and the loader reads the
  value from the file itself, so the runtime uses the exact f32.
  The dissection's printed 0.1961 is a 4-decimal display rounding
  of the same value. No discrepancy.
- Neighbouring value, for the record: kv[14]
  `muse-glimmer.final_logit_softcapping` = 20.0 exactly (f32
  bits `0x41a00000`), matching the softcap 20.0 the config doc
  states.

## Proof 1 (T-9.13 sampling parity over the socket): PASS

## The T-9.16 defects this run caught, and their fixes

The first chat request of the run failed before generation, and
the two defects below are why. Both were real defects in the
T-9.16 implementation scope; both are fixed minimally and
committed; proof 4 at the end of this note is the re-run that
passes against llama.cpp.

### Defect 1: the renderer could not render the model's own template (fixed in 9379364)

The platform answered the first chat request with a named
`chat_template_error`: `chattemplate: unsupported construct:
{% %}`. The Glimmer file's template is the full ATEM Jinja
template (9,992 chars, now kept as the renderer fixture
platform/internal/chattemplate/testdata/glimmer-atem.jinja): it
uses macros, `namespace()` state, `{% set %}` including
namespace attribute mutation, `defined` tests, `join` /
`replace` / `lower` filters, and a header comment whose text
contains tag lookalikes. The bounded renderer from 311fa1b
covered none of that, so the file's own template was outside
the subset.

Fix (commit 9379364): the renderer now supports `{# comments #}`,
macros, set including namespace attribute mutation, general
`{% for x in expr %}` with loop.index / index0 / first / last /
length and pair targets, value-typed expressions with
undefined-name semantics (falsy, answers `is defined`, refuses
by name when printed), list and mapping literals, dynamic
subscripts, dict.get / str.split / dict.items, the tests
defined, none, string, boolean, number, mapping and iterable,
inline conditionals, and the trim / lower / replace / join
filters. Constructs still outside the subset (length and tojson
filters, unknown method calls, printing a boolean) still refuse
by name. The real template renders byte-exact in unit tests.

### Defect 2: every chat prompt ran with two BOS ids (fixed in 819b1ae)

With the renderer fixed, a chat request reached the engine, and
the engine's logged prompt ids began **[200000, 200000,
200022, ...]**: the rendered template starts with the bos_token
text, which tokenizes to the BOS id 200000, and the engine then
prepended the BOS id again because the file sets
add_bos_token. llama.cpp's tokenizer drops the duplicate in
exactly this case (llama-vocab.cpp), so our ids could never
have matched llama.cpp's until this was fixed.

Fix (commit 819b1ae): a shared `assemble_prompt_ids` helper in
crates/itak-engine prepends BOS only when the tokenized body
does not already begin with it, used by generate and embed
alike. Unit-covered (prepend, already-present, not-asked,
no-BOS-id, empty body); cargo test -p itak-engine 30/30. The
post-fix engine log for the same request begins [200000,
200022, ...]: one BOS.

### Defect 3: the environment lacked strftime_now, so the rendered prompt missed the Current date line (fixed in af21f92)

Proof 4's first comparison (after fixes 1 and 2) put our 52 ids
next to llama.cpp's 63 for the same messages. The two sequences
were identical everywhere except one 11-id segment in
llama.cpp's system block: `\nCurrent date: 2026-10-31.`. The
ATEM template prints that line when a `current_date` variable
is supplied OR when `strftime_now` is defined in the
environment (template lines 115-118). llama.cpp's minja runtime
defines `strftime_now` from the host clock; our environment
defined neither variable nor function, so the guarded branch
rendered nothing, silently.

Fix (commit af21f92): the renderer registers `strftime_now` as
a global builtin, mirroring the reference environment. It
answers the defined test, formats the host clock through a
strftime subset (%Y %y %m %d %H %M %S %j %%), and refuses
unknown specifiers and printing the function itself by name.
Params.Now pins the clock for tests; the Glimmer golden now
carries the date line with a pinned date, and the
caller-system golden is unchanged (the date block lives in the
template's default-system branch only).

## Verdicts

- T-9.13 (sampling parity over the socket): **PASS.** Two
  seeded sampled requests produced identical token streams
  [13796, 24, 290, 392]; presence_penalty as the only change
  moved position 4 from 373 to 947 against the greedy control.
- T-9.14 (multi-slot engine): **PASS.** Two concurrent chat
  requests completed inside one engine with independent,
  prompt-correct outputs (France vs Japan), with the debug
  report showing slots=2, active=2 across 588 snapshots.
- T-9.15 (embeddings): **PASS.** cos(related) 0.899662 ranks
  above cos(unrelated) 0.370221 and 0.389486; dimension 6656,
  unit norms.
- T-9.16 (chat templating): **PASS, after three defects found
  and fixed by this run** (renderer subset 9379364, duplicate

===== FILE: bench/torch-runtime-2026-10-28.md =====
# iTaK Torch runtime benchmark, 2026-10-28

Question (David): does the recovered engine actually run, and how fast,
on models it supports, including on the ROCm stack?

## Setup

- Hardware: ubuntu-server, AMD Radeon RX 7900 XTX 24 GB (gfx1100),
  i7-12700K, 128 GB RAM, Ubuntu ROCm 7.1 system stack.
- Engine: iTaKTorchQ4 freshly built from the recovered source plus the
  original iTaKCore (sibling layout, go build exit 0), Linux amd64.
- FFI lock found by measurement: Torch's loader requires the
  llama_params_fit export, which current llama.cpp master no longer
  ships in libllama. All FFI runs therefore use the official llama.cpp
  b8398 release libs (the build Torch was written against), Vulkan and
  ROCm flavors. llama-bench comparisons use the same b8398 builds, plus
  current-master builds (build-vulkan2 / build-rocm2) as spot checks.
- Raw logs and JSONs: server ~/torch-bench-2026-10-28/results/.

## Headline

The engine runs. It loads real GGUF models through its llama.cpp FFI
path, generates coherent text, and serves its OpenAI-compatible API.
On matched stacks its speed is close to raw llama.cpp: the Go FFI
layer costs roughly 0 to 12 percent depending on model and backend.

## Generation speed (tokens/sec)

| Model | Torch CPU (default, pre-fix) | Torch Vulkan | Torch ROCm | llama-bench b8398 Vulkan | llama-bench b8398 ROCm | llama-bench master Vulkan | llama-bench master ROCm |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen2.5-0.5B Q4_K_M | 90.5 | n/a | n/a | 582.2 | 342.4 | n/a | n/a |
| Qwen2.5-1.5B Q4_K_M | 44.6 | 356.1 | 181.7 | 403.9 | 179.0 | n/a | n/a |
| DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite Q4_K_M | n/a | 182.9 | 53.9 | 235.0 | 134.2 | 268.3 | 168.0 |
| Qwen2.5-Coder-32B Q4_K_M | n/a | 0.7 (anomaly) | 26.5 | 36.8 | 26.5 | 38.4 | 36.6 |
| Devstral-Small-2-24B Q4_K_M | n/a | 43.6 | 37.8 | 44.0 | 38.2 | n/a | n/a |

Method notes: Torch 1.5B figures are its built-in bench (best of 3
prompts, fixed binary, default AutoConfig path). Other Torch figures
are single cold serve completions (128 tokens, temp 0, same prompt)
from the server's own [perf] lines. llama-bench figures are tg128
averages over 3 repetitions at -ngl 999. Serve numbers and bench
numbers are not perfectly matched methods; treat serve rows as
approximate.

## Findings

1. AMD detection bug (FIXED and pushed, iTaKTorchQ4 commit c66059a).
   detectLinux never read AMD VRAM (only nvidia-smi provided VRAM), so
   every AMD card probed as 0 MiB, AutoConfig concluded "iGPU only"
   and forced CPU-only. Fix reads mem_info_vram_total from amdgpu
   sysfs, plus a missing AutoConfig case for an AMD card too small
   for the model. Verified on the 7900 XTX: AutoConfig now reports
   amd(24560MiB), full offload, 1.5B at 356 tok/s Vulkan versus the
   broken 44.6 tok/s CPU default. David had no AMD card to test with
   when this was written.
2. Vulkan + Qwen2.5-Coder-32B through Torch serve collapsed to
   0.7 tok/s (128 tokens in 2m51s) and the HTTP response was lost
   (curl exit 52, empty reply) even though the scheduler logged the
   request as processed. The same model on the same stack does
   26.5 tok/s via Torch ROCm and 36.8 via llama-bench Vulkan.
   Undiagnosed; needs its own investigation.
3. DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite via Torch ROCm serve: 53.9 tok/s versus
   134.2 for llama-bench on the identical stack. Vulkan serve is
   closer (182.9 vs 235.0). Undiagnosed.
4. Native GOTensor (pure Go) path: loads Qwen2.5-0.5B in 5.4 s, then
   generation dies with "context deadline exceeded" and produces no
   output. Demo grade, consistent with the code read (char-level
   tokenizer, no KV cache). The FFI path is the production path.
5. Stack comparison on this card (llama-bench): Vulkan beats ROCm
   nearly everywhere at b8398; current-master ROCm closes much of
   the gap (DeepSeek 168.0 vs b8398 ROCm 134.2; Coder-32B 36.6 vs
   26.5). Vulkan remains the serving pick on this hardware.
6. Real output proof: Torch serve returned a correct, coherent
   explanation of transformer attention from Qwen2.5-1.5B. Cosmetic
   defect: spaces render as the BPE "Ġ" glyph in its JSON responses,
   a detokenizer piece-join bug in the response assembly.

## Pre-existing issues noted, not caused by the fix

- Full pkg/torch test suite panics in cluster_coordinator.go swarm
  tests; the pristine pre-fix tree fails identically.
- go vet reports two lock-copy warnings in server_endpoints.go.

===== END FILE: bench/torch-runtime-2026-10-28.md =====

Full profile file as written:

```
# wgpu-compute calibration profile
# Measured on the adapter named below by the calibrate_profile
# example; construction applies it only to that exact adapter
# and driver. Hand edits are read back through the same
# parsers the WGPU_COMPUTE_MMV_* env overrides use.
format_version=1
adapter_name=AMD Radeon RX 7900 XTX (RADV NAVI31)
adapter_backend=Vulkan
adapter_driver=radv
adapter_driver_info=Mesa 26.0.8-1ubuntu0.3
mmv_max_rows=16
band_q4k_attn=1,6-12
band_q4k_ffn=2-12
band_q4k_kv=1-2,4-6,16
band_q5k_attn=2-16
band_q5k_ffn=1-16
band_q5k_kv=1
band_q6k_attn=2-12
band_q6k_ffn=2-12
band_q6k_kv=4-12
```

Derived vs shipped, cell by cell (ceiling matches: 16 = 16):

| cell | derived | shipped | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| q4k attn | 1,6-12 | 6-12 | differs only at batch 1 (see artifact note) |
| q4k ffn | 2-12 | 2,4-12 | DIFFERS: row 3 now a win |
| q4k kv | 1-2,4-6,16 | 2-3 | DIFFERS: rows 3 lost, 4-6 and 16 gained |
| q5k attn | 2-16 | 2-16 | match |
| q5k ffn | 1-16 | 3-16 | DIFFERS: rows 1-2 gained |
| q5k kv | 1 (closed) | 16 | DIFFERS: inverted, win at 16 now closed |
| q6k attn | 2-12 | 2-12 | match |
| q6k ffn | 2-12 | 2-12 | match |
| q6k kv | 4-12 | 12 | DIFFERS: widens to 4-12 |

So 3 of 9 cells match exactly. Two honest qualifications
on the differing cells:

1. **Batch-1 entries are an artifact, identified.** Three
   derived cells (q4k attn, q4k kv, q5k ffn) include batch
   1. The MMV arm pins its bands to 2-16, so at batch 1
   both arms dispatch the identical GEMV form; the diag
   census of the run confirms it (the batch-1 GEMV
   dispatch count is 50 per shape, 25 per arm, with zero
   MMV dispatches at batch 1). A batch-1 "win" under the
   0.98x rule is therefore inter-arm timing drift between
   two sequential arms measuring the same code path, not
   a form win. Discounting batch 1, q4k attn matches the
   shipped cell on every batch that can route. The q5k
   ffn row-2 gain and the q4k ffn row-3 gain are not
   explained by this artifact.
2. **No per-cell medians are claimed.** The calibrator's
   printed output is the derived table only; it publishes
   no per-cell medians or ratios. The session mined the
   diag dispatch stream for per-dispatch medians, but
   those do not reproduce ProjBench's per-call derivation
   on several cells (they disagree in both directions,
   e.g. q5k kv and q4k attn at batches 9 and 12, because
   a ProjBench cell figure aggregates the whole prepared
   call, not the single product dispatch). The mined
   numbers are therefore not reported as evidence for or
   against any cell. What stands is the derivation
   itself, run at verdict reps on the same card and
   driver the shipped table came from: the kv cells and
   the two ffn boundary rows genuinely re-measured
   differently this run, and any future table change
   should be decided with a sweep CSV beside it, the way
   the shipped table was.

## Leg 2, coopmat v2 / K24: decision rule MET on the numbers

## Leg 5, n-gram: mechanism proven on the real file; prose acceptance is near zero, repetitive acceptance is real

Wave18 DFlash record for comparison: depth 1 effective 22.07
tok/s, depth 6 effective 16.80 tok/s, both identity-passing.

- (a) GPU arms, --drafter=ngram, default prompt, both mode, 64
  tokens. Depth 1: IDENTITY PASS + GOLDEN PASS; spec stats
  rounds=60 proposed=6 accepted=3 acceptance_rate=0.500
  tokens_per_round=1.05; effective 34.61 tok/s, all-in 33.70.
  Depth 6: IDENTITY PASS + GOLDEN PASS; rounds=58 proposed=24
  accepted=5 acceptance_rate=0.208 tokens_per_round=1.09;
  effective 31.45 tok/s, all-in 30.74. Honest reading: on this
  prose prompt the proposer almost never fires (6 proposals in
  60 rounds at depth 1), so both rates are the plain-decode
  floor (about 34.5 tok/s), not a speculation win. They read
  above the DFlash record only because DFlash pays its about
  40.6 ms draft forward every round and the n-gram proposer
  pays nothing. Where the generated stream itself turns
  repetitive (the capital prompt loops), proposals rise (24 at
  depth 6) but acceptance stays low (0.208).
- (b) Repetitive-prompt arm, depth 6 (a six-times-repeated
  instruction block, 113 prompt tokens): IDENTITY PASS (GOLDEN
  prints only for the default prompt). Spec stats rounds=20
  proposed=55 accepted=43 acceptance_rate=0.782
  tokens_per_round=3.15; effective 51.12 tok/s (generate phase),
  all-in 33.21 (the short run's prefill and session build
  dominate the all-in figure). This is the honest best case and
  it works: on truly repetitive text the proposer pays off
  (51.12 vs the about 34.5 plain floor and vs DFlash depth-6
  16.80), at zero draft cost.
- (c) CPU-driver acceptance run (spec_generate --drafter=ngram
  on the real file): CUT, stated plainly. The baseline session
  measured CPU walls of 2,256-4,802 s per 16-token prompt; a
  64-token both-mode CPU run is a 5-10 hour job that would hold
  the phase lock and outlive this session. The proposer code
  path is already proven on the real file by the GPU arms above
  (identity token-identical at both depths) and by the fixture
  and recorded-stream tests in the n-gram lanes. The CPU arm
  remains owed if a future session wants it for completeness.
- Framing, per the notes: acceptance collapses on non-repetitive
  text; n-gram complements DFlash by never paying the draft
  forward, it does not replace it.

(COOPMAT=0 and MMQ_SPLITK=off).

### 1,022 tokens, 3 rounds each, interleaved A B A B A B

- Arm A walls: 3,348 / 3,371 / 3,539 ms, median 3,371 ms.
  Argmax 7235 @ 12.230860 in all reps. K24 line 1,718.678 /
  1,729.950 / 1,768.165 ms @ 2,912; K14 split line 700.451 /
  706.577 ms @ 832; reduce ~3.1 ms @ 832.
- Arm B walls: 6,678 / 6,471 / 6,433 ms, median 6,471 ms.
  Argmax 7235 @ 12.233533 in all reps. K13 line 4,213.549 /
  4,104.827 / 4,089.647 ms @ 2,912.
- Combined wall improvement: about -48% (3,371 vs 6,471 ms).
  Placed against the wave20 single-feature figures WITHOUT
  summing them: K24 alone was -36% of wall and split-K alone
  -18% at this shape. The combined figure is larger than
  either single because the control here loses both wins at
  once, and the two wins only partly overlap: the Q4_K part
  overlaps exactly as the panel predicted (split-K does not
  stack on the coopmat rung), while the Q6_K part does not
  overlap (the K14 line roughly halves, ~1,310 ms plain to
  ~703 ms split, inside the defaults arm). Kernel-line ratio
  K24 vs K13 on medians: about 2.38x (~1,730 vs ~4,105 ms).

### 8,202 tokens, two interleaved rounds

- Arm A walls: 46,291 / 45,975 / 46,047 ms (three reps; round 2
  contributed two), median 46,047 ms. Census: k24_q4k_coopmat
  23,296 @ 14,033.359 / 13,956.950 ms; k14_q6k_mmq_split 6,656
  @ 5,771.867 / 5,728.037 ms; splitk_reduce 6,656 @ ~25 ms.
- Arm B walls: 68,116 / 68,909 ms, median 68,512 ms. Census:
  k13_q4k_mmq 23,296 @ 31,857.392 / 32,235.388 ms;
  k14_q6k_mmq 6,656 @ 10,126.004 / 10,265.550 ms.
- Combined wall improvement: about -33% (46,047 vs 68,512 ms).
- The winner at this shape differs by configuration; see the
  divergence section below.

## The 8,202-token argmax divergence: investigated, verdict below

At 1,022 tokens every configuration measured (defaults, both
rollbacks, control) agrees on winner 7235. At 8,202 tokens the
configurations divide deterministically:

- Defaults (K24 + split-K 4): id=589 @ 9.131593, reproduced
  bit-identically in three prefill reps and in two independent
  full-forward harnesses (prefill_profile's argmax tail and
  glimmer_generate --gpu-argmax, which share no readback code).
- Coopmat off only (split-K still on): id=589 @ 9.004866.
- Split-K off only (coopmat still on): id=589 @ 9.109748.
- Pre-flip control (both off): id=7235 @ 8.854632,
  bit-identical to wave20's f32 off-arm value at this shape.

So EACH flip alone moves the final-position winner from 7235 to
589, at three distinct logit values; the two flips do not need
each other to do it. 589 was also wave20's f16 winner at 8,202
tokens, but at a different logit (9.080180); KV_F16 was
scrubbed/unset in every wave21 arm and the leg 1(a) manifest
carries the resolved f32 config, so this is not the f16 path
engaging.

VERDICT, stated plainly: this is a near-tie break, not a proven
defect, and not a proven non-defect either. The fox prompt is
periodic with a 10-token period, so after 8,202 tokens the
final position is a near-tie between period-continuation
candidates, and any change in accumulation order (K24's integer
coopmat product, split-K's reassociated reduction, each
documented as reassociation-class drift) can break the tie
differently. Both configurations are internally deterministic
to the last bit across reps and across harnesses, and the
control reproduces wave20's value exactly, which rules out
nondeterminism and rules out a staging error. What this session
did NOT do: a per-layer or per-logit comparison at this shape
that would prove the two winners' true logit gap is inside the
reassociation noise band. The identity and golden gates do not
cover this shape (they run the 7-token prompt). The honest
residual: at long context, the shipped defaults' greedy winner
on a periodic prompt differs from the pre-flip winner, cause
attributed to accumulation-order sensitivity on a near-tie,
with a direct logit-gap measurement at 8,202 tokens still owed
if a stronger verdict is wanted. No default was changed on the
strength of this; the flips' evidence at every gated shape
stands.

## Leg 5, gate.sh on the card: RAN; 1 test failure, root-caused

bench/gate.sh, first adapter-present execution. Exit code 1.
Summary lines verbatim:

    gate: passed 749, failed 1, ignored 1; skipped 0 adapter
    (adapter present: expectation 0), 6 other (named exceptions,
    not gated)
    gate: FAIL: cargo test exited 101 with 1 failed

The Category J criterion is met on its own terms: the wrapper
enumerated the adapter, and adapter skips are ZERO; the device
tests executed on the card instead of skipping. The 6 "other"
skips are env-arm skips by design, each named in the output:
two dflash diag arms needing DIAG_OUT set; three K21F routing
pins needing their env arms (WGPU_COMPUTE_MMV_MAX_ROWS closing
value, WGPU_COMPUTE_K21F_HEAD=0, WGPU_COMPUTE_DIAG=timing); one
further named exception of the same class. None is an adapter
skip and none is a missing-file skip. shellcheck is not
installed on this server; gate.sh's header NOT RUN note stands;
nothing was installed.

The one failure: resident_session_prefix_store_round_trip, in
the same test binary as leg 4. It panicked at
crates/wgpu-compute/tests/prefix_kv_session.rs:401,
"capture and store after the cold prefill", with the f16
guard's own refusal: "the session's KV storage is f16
(WGPU_COMPUTE_KV_F16=1)". Root cause, established by controlled
reruns in this session:

- The f16 switch is resolved per backend construction from the
  process env (compute.rs, WgpuCompute::new). Inside one test
  binary the two tests run on parallel threads sharing one
  process env. The guard test sets WGPU_COMPUTE_KV_F16=1
  (prefix_kv_session.rs:698) and removes it only at its end
  (line 805), minutes later on card time. The round-trip test
  never touches the variable; a backend it constructs inside
  the guard test's f16 window resolves f16 storage, and its
  capture is then refused, correctly, by the guard.
- Serialized reruns: with --exact, each test passes alone on
  the card (guard 45.31 s; round trip passes). Together in one
  binary invocation they fail the same way as in the gate
  (reproduced twice: in gate.sh and in a direct two-test run).
- The guard itself is not implicated: it fired exactly as
  designed, on a session that really was f16. The defect is in
  the test file: process-global env choreography between two
  tests in one binary is racy under parallel test threads.

This is a test-harness defect at cb579ad, invisible on
adapterless machines (both tests skip there) and visible only
when the suite runs on a card with default parallelism. The
fix (serialize the two tests, or move the f16-window test to
its own binary) is a later lane; no code was changed here.
Consequence for the standing record: the workspace suite is
749/750 on the card at cb579ad, and the one failure is this
race, not a product defect.
